title: Find Your Feet
greet: Hey, it’s Lensy. Spoiler: nobody has the future figured out, not even the highlight reels you scroll. Loosen the comparison trap; your worth was never your CV.

badge.title: Find Your Feet 🛤️
badge.blurb: You can see past the highlight reel, know uncertainty is normal, setbacks are information not verdicts, and your worth was never your CV. One step at a time. 🌱

helpLine: Comparison and placement pressure are heavy; you don’t carry them alone. If it’s too much: Tele-MANAS 14416 (24/7), or someone you trust.
reassure: No one has it figured out. Setbacks are information, not verdicts; failure is a comma, not a full stop. If it’s heavy: Tele-MANAS 14416. 🌱

scenarios.hook: "Everyone else has it figured out; I'm the only one behind."

myth.un: Everyone else has it figured out; I'm the only one behind.
myth.re: No one has it figured out; you're comparing your behind-the-scenes to their highlight reel.
myth.why: People post wins, not the doubts and rejections.

scenarios.relearn: No one has it figured out; you're comparing your insides to others' highlight reels.

scenarios.hook: Sort: the real picture, or the highlight reel?

items.text: The fear that it won't work out

scenarios.relearn: Offers and captions are the highlight reel; the rejections and worry behind them are the real picture.

scenarios.hook: Scrolling everyone's placement and success posts is spiking your anxiety.

steps.prompt: Another offer-letter post appears and your chest tightens. What do you do?

options.text: Keep scrolling to see who else got in
options.then: You find eight more posts, and your chest gets tighter.

options.text: Like them all, then message friends about how behind you feel
options.then: The friends send sad faces, and the feed is still open.

options.text: Close the app and step away for a while
options.then: You drink some water, and your breathing slows.

options.text: Post a small win of your own to keep up
options.then: A few likes come in, and you keep checking for more.

steps.why: Stepping away gives your body a chance to settle before you decide anything.

steps.prompt: You have a free hour tomorrow. What do you do with it?

options.text: Read stories about how other people got placed
options.then: You collect ten stories, and each one makes yours feel smaller.

options.text: Check the feed to make sure you haven't missed anything
options.then: You find nothing new, and the hour is gone.

options.text: Work on one thing for your own path, like your CV
options.then: You fix two lines on your CV, and it feels like progress.

options.text: Plan how to beat everyone else's timeline
options.then: The plan gets big, and the pressure grows with it.

steps.why: An hour on something of your own adds real progress, unlike time spent watching others.

steps.prompt: A friend says she's tired of the feeds too. What do you do?

options.text: Say everyone else seems fine, so you'll stay on it
options.then: She nods, and the two of you keep scrolling.

options.text: Say you'll quit all social media forever
options.then: She looks doubtful, and the plan doesn't last the weekend.

options.text: Agree on a daily limit and check in with each other
options.then: The next evening, she texts to say she stayed under it.

options.text: Change the subject and never bring it up again
options.then: The feed keeps pulling at you alone.

steps.why: A shared limit is easier to keep, and it reminds you that you aren't the only one.

scenarios.debrief: Curated success feeds fuel comparison anxiety, and stepping back to refocus on your own path helps.
scenarios.relearn: Step back from success feeds and refocus on your own path.

scenarios.hook: "Comparing myself to others pushes me to do better."

myth.un: Comparison pushes me to do better.
myth.re: Comparison mostly fuels anxiety and shame; your own values-based steps drive you better.
myth.why: Inadequacy is a poor long-term motivator.

scenarios.relearn: Comparison mostly fuels anxiety; your own values-based steps motivate you better.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two comparison-thief thoughts to catch (the rest hold your own path).

scene.text: "I'll never measure up to them"
"My path is my own"
"Their highlight reel isn't my reality"
"If they're winning, I'm losing"
"I can be glad for them and steady in myself"

scenarios.why: 'Never measure up' and 'if they win, I lose' are the comparison thief; owning your path and naming highlight reels isn't.
scenarios.relearn: Comparison is the thief of joy, and never a fair fight against an edit.

scenarios.hook: Sort: eases comparison anxiety, or feeds it?

items.text: Refreshing the placement list all day

scenarios.relearn: Curating your feed, honest talk and breaks ease comparison; stalking achievements and like-counting feed it.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Meher shares big career news, and you feel a pang of comparison.
scenarios.setup: She finds you outside the library with her phone in hand.

steps.prompt: Meher says: "I got the job! Can you believe it?"

options.text: "Oh. Nice. Good for you."
options.then: Her smile dims. "Thanks. I thought you'd be happier."

options.text: "So everyone is getting jobs except me."
options.then: She pauses. "That's not what I meant."

options.text: "That's brilliant. I'm genuinely happy for you!"
options.then: She beams. "Thank you! I still can't believe it."

options.text: "You were lucky. Some of us actually had to work for it."
options.then: She looks stung. "That's unfair."

steps.why: Being warm about her win costs you nothing, and her good news isn't a verdict on you.

steps.prompt: Meher says: "Honestly, I almost didn't apply. I was so nervous."

options.text: "You shouldn't have been nervous. It was obvious you'd get it."
options.then: She shrugs. "Well, it didn't feel obvious."

options.text: "At least you had the option to be nervous."
options.then: She goes quiet. "I guess that's true."

options.text: "I'd have been nervous too. What made you apply?"
options.then: She thinks. "My brother pushed me."

options.text: "Right. Anyway, I need to go now."
options.then: She catches your arm. "Wait. Before you go."

steps.why: Being curious about how she did it lets you hear her side, and you may learn from it.

steps.prompt: Meher asks: "What about you? Any news?"

options.text: "Oh, I have something big coming up too."
options.then: She smiles. "Really? What is it?"

options.text: "No. I'm always the one left behind."
options.then: She frowns. "That's not true."

options.text: "Not yet. I'm still working out my next step."
options.then: She nods. "It's okay. I was too, last month."

options.text: "Not really. Let's only talk about you."
options.then: She hesitates. "Are you sure? You seem off."

steps.why: Honest, calm news about yourself is easier than a made-up story or a gloomy one.

scenarios.relearn: Be warm at a friend's success. Their win isn't your loss.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two comparison-trap thoughts to catch (the rest are truer reads).

scene.text: "They're all ahead of me"
"Everyone's timeline is different"
"I must be failing if they're winning"
"Their win takes nothing from me"
"I'm comparing my insides to their highlights"

scenarios.why: 'They're all ahead' and 'I'm failing if they win' are comparison traps; different timelines and 'win takes nothing' aren't.
scenarios.relearn: 'Everyone's ahead' and 'their win means my failure' are comparison traps.

scenarios.hook: "If I haven't succeeded by a certain age, I've failed at life."

myth.un: If I haven't succeeded by a certain age, I've failed at life.
myth.re: There's no universal timeline; everyone's path unfolds differently and at its own pace.
myth.why: Life isn't a race with one finish line.

scenarios.relearn: There's no universal timeline; paths unfold differently and at their own pace.

scenarios.hook: Your mother keeps holding up a cousin who "has it sorted".
scenarios.setup: She brings it up again over dinner.

steps.prompt: Your mother says: "Look at Priya. She's settled in a good job already. And you?"

options.text: "She had a lot more help than I've had."
options.then: Your mother frowns. "That's not nice."

options.text: "You're right, Mummy. I'm really far behind."
options.then: She sighs. "I didn't say that, beta."

options.text: "We're on different paths. I'm okay on mine."
options.then: She pauses. "Hm. Okay on what?"

options.text: "Priya, Priya, Priya. Is she all you ever talk about?"
options.then: Her face tightens. "Don't speak to me like that."

steps.why: A calm sentence holds your path without putting your cousin down.

steps.prompt: She says: "I only want you to be secure. Is that wrong?"

options.text: "You don't care what I actually want."
options.then: She steps back. "That's not fair, beta."

options.text: "Fine. I'll do whatever you think is right."
options.then: She nods, but looks uneasy.

options.text: "No. I want that too. Mine may look different."
options.then: She studies you. "Different how?"

options.text: "I'll be secure soon. I promise."
options.then: She smiles, and you feel the weight of it.

steps.why: Sharing the goal of security, and that yours looks different, keeps her on your side.

steps.prompt: Your mother asks: "So what are you doing about it?"

options.text: "Nothing. Let's not talk about it."
options.then: She sighs. "Not talking about it is what worries me."

options.text: "I'll get a job like hers as soon as possible."
options.then: She nods. "Good. Start looking."

options.text: "I'm building skills I care about. Want to see?"
options.then: She raises her eyebrows. "You have a plan? Show me."

options.text: "Why do you always ask me this every time?"
options.then: Her voice rises. "Because I care."

steps.why: Naming one small step you care about shows her your path is real.

scenarios.relearn: Hold your own path. A relative's success isn't your yardstick.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a fair comparison, or an unfair one?

items.text: You now vs you last year
Your effort vs your own last attempt
Your day one vs their year five

scenarios.relearn: Measuring against your past self and your goals is fair; against others' finish or highlights isn't.

scenarios.hook: You realise your feed is mostly people who make you feel behind.

steps.prompt: You scroll for a minute and notice how tight your shoulders feel. What do you do?

options.text: Keep them and push through to toughen up
options.then: The tension stays, and so does the list of accounts.

options.text: Stay on those accounts so you don't miss out
options.then: You don't miss anything, and you feel worse.

options.text: Follow even more high achievers to push yourself
options.then: The feed fills with wins, and the tightness spreads.

options.text: Mute accounts that leave you feeling small
options.then: Your feed goes quieter, and your shoulders drop a little.

steps.why: What you look at every day shapes how you feel, and you can choose it.

steps.prompt: A friend sends you a list of accounts she likes. Which kind do you follow?

options.text: Motivational quote pages with big promises
options.then: The quotes are catchy, and they leave you feeling the same.

options.text: Big names posting their wins and offers
options.then: The faces change, and the feeling of being behind stays.

options.text: Mentors and people who share honest work
options.then: The first post you see is someone describing a failed attempt.

options.text: None, so there's less to compare with
options.then: Nothing new comes in, and by night you're scrolling out of habit.

steps.why: Honest, real posts keep you learning without pressure to perform.

steps.prompt: A week on, a close friend posts a proud achievement. How do you take it?

options.text: Mute your friend too, just to be safe for now
options.then: The feed is calmer, and the friendship is a little further away.

options.text: Like it, then spend a whole hour comparing
options.then: The hour passes, and the comparison leaves you tired.

options.text: Celebrate her, and let the pang pass
options.then: You text her congrats, and the pang fades by dinner.

options.text: Stop following friends who do really well
options.then: The feed gets quiet, and so does your circle.

steps.why: You can be glad for her and feel the pang, and neither cancels the other.

scenarios.debrief: Your feed shapes your mood, so curating it away from shame-triggers is real self-care.
scenarios.relearn: Curate your feed toward what inspires, away from what shames you.

scenarios.hook: "The people who seem to have it all together are never anxious."
scenarios.relearn: The people you envy are often quietly envying someone too.

myth.un: The people who seem to have it all together are never anxious.
myth.re: The people you envy are often quietly envying someone too; almost everyone feels behind sometimes.
myth.why: Outer confidence hides inner doubt.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Arjun is crushed, comparing himself to everyone's success posts.
scenarios.setup: He holds his phone out to you on the bench.

steps.prompt: Arjun says: "Look at them all. I'm so far behind."

options.text: "Yeah, you're kind of falling behind, honestly."
options.then: His face falls. "Wow. Thanks."

options.text: "Stop looking at it. You're being silly."
options.then: He mutters: "It's not silly to me."

options.text: "That's just their highlight reel."
options.then: He looks at the phone again. "Hm. Maybe."

options.text: "They all had help, so it doesn't count."
options.then: He shrugs. "That doesn't make me feel better."

steps.why: Their posts are edited highlights, and he can see his own path is different.

steps.prompt: Arjun asks: "How are they all so sure of everything?"

options.text: "Maybe they really are better planned than us."
options.then: He nods glumly. "Yeah."

options.text: "Just act confident, like they do."
options.then: He sighs. "I don't know how."

options.text: "Then let's make a bigger plan than theirs."
options.then: He looks tired. "That sounds exhausting."

options.text: "Most are scared too. They don't post that."
options.then: He laughs a little. "Really?"

steps.why: Most people feel unsure, and they just don't post that part.

steps.prompt: Arjun asks: "So what do I do instead of scrolling?"

options.text: "Delete every app tonight, for good."
options.then: He winces. "That feels too much."

options.text: "Keep scrolling, but try not to feel anything."
options.then: He shakes his head. "That's not possible."

options.text: "Wait until you feel better, then decide."
options.then: He sighs. "I don't know when that'll be."

options.text: "Pick one thing for this week. Phones down."
options.then: He pockets his phone. "Okay. What's first?"

steps.why: One small thing, done together with phones down, gives him something real to do.

scenarios.relearn: Remind a friend that success posts are highlight reels, not the whole story.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a kind, true thought, or a comparison distortion?
scenarios.relearn: 'My own progress' and 'their path isn't mine' are true; 'everyone's better' and 'hopelessly behind' are distortions.

scenarios.hook: "I need my whole life and career planned out right now."

myth.un: I need my whole life planned out now.
myth.re: Uncertainty at this age is normal; small next steps beat a perfect master plan.
myth.why: No one can plan a whole life in advance.

scenarios.relearn: Uncertainty is normal; small next steps beat a perfect master plan.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the honest headline, no one really has it all figured out, even the confident ones. Believe it?
scenarios.affirm: It's genuinely true: almost everyone is figuring it out as they go, including the confident ones.
scenarios.relearn: No one really has it all figured out, even the confident ones.

scenarios.hook: You feel panicked because you don't know exactly what you want to do.

steps.prompt: Your roommate asks about your plans and the panic rises. What do you do?

options.text: Say "I don't know yet" and stay curious
options.then: Your roommate nods. "Same, honestly." The panic drops a notch.

options.text: Name a career you've heard is safe
options.then: Your roommate says it sounds sensible. You feel queasy about a plan you never chose.

options.text: Change the subject and avoid the question
options.then: Your roommate lets it go, and the question follows you to bed.

options.text: Pick a field tonight just to end the panic
options.then: You write a field on a sticky note. The relief lasts about an hour.

steps.why: Not knowing yet is normal. Curiosity calms panic better than a forced answer.

steps.prompt: A few days later a senior mentions a club fair. You still feel unsure. What do you do?

options.text: Visit two stalls just to look around
options.then: You come back with a flyer and one new question to think about.

options.text: Skip it until you know your field
options.then: The fair goes by. You still have no sense of what interests you.

options.text: Sign up for everything so you miss nothing
options.then: Your week fills up fast, and the panic comes back in a new form.

options.text: Join whichever club everyone calls the best
options.then: You join, and feel oddly flat at the first meeting.

steps.why: Sampling a little gives real information. Skipping or overloading does not.

steps.prompt: Weeks on, a cousin calls to ask what you've decided. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're exploring and share a curiosity
options.then: Your cousin says, "Honestly, that sounds more honest than my plan."

options.text: Give a confident answer just to end the call
options.then: Your cousin sounds impressed. You hang up feeling like you've lied.

options.text: Say you're too confused and change the topic
options.then: Your cousin pauses, unsure whether to worry about you.

options.text: Say you're waiting for the answer to appear
options.then: Your cousin laughs and suggests you don't wait too long.

steps.why: Saying you're exploring is honest and keeps the pressure off you.

scenarios.debrief: Not knowing yet is a normal, workable place to be. Exploring is part of the process.
scenarios.relearn: It's okay not to know yet; let yourself explore.

scenarios.hook: Match the realistic truth to the pressure it answers.
scenarios.relearn: Changing direction and pivoting are realistic; 'first job decides all' and 'sorted now' are unfair pressure.

pairs.left: It's okay not to know yet
Small steps beat a master plan

scenarios.hook: "Changing my mind about my path means I've wasted time."

myth.un: Changing my path means I wasted time.
myth.re: Exploring and pivoting is how most people find a fit; nothing learned is wasted.
myth.why: Detours often teach the most.

scenarios.relearn: Changing your path isn't wasted time; exploring is how a fit is found.

scenarios.hook: You're at a friend's gathering and have no neat answer about your future.
scenarios.setup: Vikram, a friend's cousin, turns to you with a smile.

steps.prompt: Vikram asks: "So what's your plan after graduation?"

options.text: "I'm still exploring, and I'm fine with that."
options.then: Vikram nods. "Honestly, that's more honest than most answers."

options.text: "Oh, I have the whole thing mapped out, honestly."
options.then: "Nice. Tell me more." You hunt for details that aren't there.

options.text: "No idea at all. I'm a complete mess, to be honest."
options.then: Vikram laughs, unsure. "Oh. Relax. It's not that serious."

options.text: "Why does everyone keep asking me that?"
options.then: Vikram raises his hands. "Sorry. Just making conversation."

steps.why: 'I'm exploring' is a valid answer. You don't need a master plan.

steps.prompt: Vikram says: "I had no plan at your age. I just picked something and stuck to it."

options.text: "That worked for you. I'm trying things first."
options.then: Vikram grins. "Fair. Different roads."

options.text: "Maybe I should just pick something, then, fast."
options.then: "Well, think about it first," he says, suddenly unsure.

options.text: "So I'm already late, aren't I? Is that it?"
options.then: Vikram blinks. "That's not what I meant at all."

options.text: "That sounds like a silly way to live, honestly."
options.then: Vikram's smile fades. The chat cools a little.

steps.why: Their way worked for them. Yours can look different.

steps.prompt: Vikram asks: "So what are you doing in the meantime?"

options.text: "Talking to people and a short course. Want to hear more?"
options.then: He leans in. "Yes, tell me. I might know someone."

options.text: "Nothing yet. I'm waiting to see what happens."
options.then: He nods slowly. "Hmm. Don't wait too long, yaar."

options.text: "A bit of everything, honestly. Nothing in particular."
options.then: He smiles politely. The conversation drifts to cricket.

options.text: "Stacking up certificates that look good on paper."
options.then: Vikram laughs. "Do you actually like any of them?"

steps.why: Naming one real thing you're trying makes 'exploring' concrete.

scenarios.relearn: 'I'm exploring' is a valid answer; you don't need a neat master plan.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a career is a long, winding road, not a single leap you must nail at 21. Easier breathing?
scenarios.affirm: A working life is decades long and winding; you don't have to nail it all at twenty-one.
scenarios.relearn: A career is a long, winding road, not one leap you must nail at 21.

scenarios.hook: Match the healthy response to uncertainty to the anxious one it replaces.
scenarios.relearn: Trying things and asking around is a healthy response to uncertainty; freezing or panic-applying isn't.

pairs.left: Talk it through with a mentor

scenarios.hook: You feel behind because you haven't specialised like some peers.

steps.prompt: A classmate already has a niche and a portfolio, and you have a bit of everything. What do you tell yourself?

options.text: My mix of interests is a shape too, not a flaw
options.then: You still feel a twinge, but you stop calling yourself a mess.

options.text: Early specialists always win, so I've lost
options.then: You close your notes and feel far behind a race you never signed up for.

options.text: I'll pick a niche by Friday to catch up
options.then: You choose one at random. By Sunday it already feels wrong.

options.text: I'll avoid talking about it until I'm sorted
options.then: You skip a few meet-ups and the silence makes the worry bigger.

steps.why: Generalists and late bloomers thrive too. There is no single shape.

steps.prompt: Later, a faculty member asks what your focus is. What do you do?

options.text: Describe your range and what you enjoy now
options.then: The faculty member nods. "That's a real starting point."

options.text: Borrow your classmate's niche as your answer
options.then: The next question exposes that it isn't yours, and you stumble.

options.text: Say you don't have one and look away, quietly
options.then: The conversation ends quickly, and you feel smaller.

options.text: Name whichever field pays the most
options.then: The faculty member asks why. You don't have a reason.

steps.why: Describing what you actually enjoy gives a real answer to build on.

steps.prompt: A senior says she only found her field in her final year. What do you take from that?

options.text: Careers come in many speeds and shapes
options.then: You relax a little. There's no single clock running on you.

options.text: She was lucky, so I can't count on it
options.then: You keep bracing for the day you fall off the clock.

options.text: It's too late for me, since I'm not her
options.then: You start measuring yourself against a story that isn't yours.

options.text: I should rush to specialise before final year
options.then: You pick in a hurry, and the hurry is what you remember.

steps.why: Different people find their field at different times.

scenarios.debrief: There's no single right speed or shape to a career; generalists and late bloomers do just fine.
scenarios.relearn: Generalists and late bloomers thrive too; there's no one right path-shape.

scenarios.hook: "If I don't get the 'right' first job, my whole future is set."

myth.un: My first job sets my whole future.
myth.re: Your first job is a starting point, not a life sentence; careers shift constantly.
myth.why: Almost no one ends where they began.

scenarios.relearn: Your first job is a starting point, not a life sentence.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: it's okay for your path to look different from the one your family imagined. Permission?
scenarios.affirm: Your path can differ from what others imagined and still be a good, valid one.
scenarios.relearn: It's okay for your path to differ from the one others imagined.

scenarios.hook: The pressure to "have it sorted" is making you anxious and stuck.

steps.prompt: You've spent the evening staring at a blank plan page. What do you do?

options.text: Trade the master plan for one small next step
options.then: You write one line. The page stops feeling like an exam.

options.text: Wait until you can see the whole path
options.then: An hour passes. The page is still blank and your chest is tighter.

options.text: Copy a plan from someone who looks sorted
options.then: You fill the page fast. Reading it back, none of it sounds like you.

options.text: Scroll until you feel calmer, then plan
options.then: The scrolling calms you for a while. The page is still blank at midnight.

steps.why: You don't need the whole map. One step is enough to start moving.

steps.prompt: Next morning one small task comes to mind, but a voice says it's too small to matter. What do you do?

options.text: Do it anyway and notice how it feels
options.then: You finish in twenty minutes, and feel a little steadier.

options.text: Add nine more steps to make it count
options.then: The list grows and the anxiety grows with it.

options.text: Skip it until you can plan the big picture
options.then: The day goes by with nothing done, and the voice gets louder.

options.text: Ask three people whether the step is worth it
options.then: Each person says something different, and you're more confused.

steps.why: A small step you actually take beats a large plan you never start.

steps.prompt: A week on, a friend says she has her whole life planned. What do you do?

options.text: Stay curious, and keep taking your own next step
options.then: She shares her plan. You take one idea and leave the rest.

options.text: Rewrite your plan to match hers
options.then: Your new plan looks impressive and feels like someone else's.

options.text: Decide she's simply more capable than you
options.then: Her certainty feels like proof against you, and your mood drops.

options.text: Tell her plans never work out
options.then: She looks hurt, and you feel oddly no lighter.

steps.why: Her certainty is about her. You can learn from it without measuring yourself.

scenarios.debrief: You don't need the whole map; a single next step is enough to start moving.
scenarios.relearn: Trade the master plan for one small next step.

scenarios.hook: Match the uncertainty truth to its reassurance.
scenarios.relearn: Most not knowing yet and figuring it out as you go is true; 'failing' and 'everyone's certain' are false.

pairs.left: Figure it out as you go

pairs.right: A compass without a fixed plan

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'I don't know yet' is the start of finding out, not a failure. Reframe it that way?
scenarios.affirm: 'I don't know yet' is simply where finding out begins; it's a beginning, not a verdict.
scenarios.relearn: 'I don't know yet' is the start of finding out, not a failure.

scenarios.hook: "A bad result or rejection means I'm a failure."

myth.un: A bad result or rejection means I'm a failure.
myth.re: Setbacks are information, not verdicts; they tell you something to adjust, not who you are.
myth.why: One outcome doesn't define you.

scenarios.relearn: Setbacks are information, not verdicts on who you are.

scenarios.hook: "If I fail this exam, my career is over."

myth.un: If I fail this exam, my career is over.
myth.re: Exam failure rarely ends a career; it's a comma, not a full stop, and often redirects you to a better fit.
myth.why: There are many routes onward.

scenarios.relearn: Exam failure is a comma, not a full stop; it often redirects to a better fit.

scenarios.hook: You got rejected from something you really wanted.

steps.prompt: The email is short and polite. What do you do first?

options.text: Skip the feeling and start fixing it right away
options.then: You make a tidy list in an hour, but the hurt is still sitting there unspoken.

options.text: Tell yourself it proves you're not good enough
options.then: The thought repeats all evening, and the day feels heavier.

options.text: Let it sting for a while, then ask what it could teach you
options.then: You take a walk, then come back with a notebook and a calmer head.

options.text: Act as if it never mattered and tell everyone you didn't care
options.then: Friends nod, but you feel the gap between what you said and what you feel.

steps.why: Feeling it first, then learning from it, turns a rejection into something you can use.

steps.prompt: A few days later, the rejection still crosses your mind. What do you do with it?

options.text: Guess what went wrong and change everything in your application
options.then: You rework it all, and can't tell which change mattered.

options.text: Push the thought away so it stops hurting
options.then: It returns at night anyway, with no lesson attached.

options.text: Ask for feedback and note what you can change
options.then: They reply with two short lines, and one of them is something you can fix.

options.text: Ask a friend who got in to tell you how they did it
options.then: Your friend shares her story kindly, but it can't tell you what your own application lacked.

steps.why: Real feedback gives you something specific to act on.

steps.prompt: Another opening comes up that is close to the first one. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it, since you were already turned down once
options.then: The deadline passes, and you wonder if the answer would have been different.

options.text: Wait until you feel fully confident before applying
options.then: Weeks go by waiting for confidence, and the window closes.

options.text: Send the same application again without changes
options.then: You send it in ten minutes, and nothing in it is different.

options.text: Apply again using what you learned
options.then: It takes an evening, and the new version reads clearer than the first.

steps.why: Trying again with what you learned is how a setback becomes progress.

scenarios.debrief: Rejection stings, but treating it as feedback to learn from is what builds resilience.
scenarios.relearn: After a rejection, feel it, learn from it, and try again.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a growth-mindset response, or a fixed one?

items.text: "This is hard, but I can improve"
"Some people are born for this; I'm not"

scenarios.relearn: 'Try a different approach', 'what can I learn' and 'I can improve' are growth; 'not capable', 'no point' and 'not born for this' are fixed.

scenarios.hook: A placement season goes badly and you feel crushed.

steps.prompt: The last company's list comes out without your name. What do you do that evening?

options.text: Tell everyone you're fine and go back to your room
options.then: The room is very quiet, and the knot in your stomach stays.

options.text: Decide right now that your future is ruined
options.then: By midnight you've imagined years of trouble that haven't happened.

options.text: Call someone you trust and say how it feels
options.then: They listen without trying to fix anything, and your chest loosens a little.

options.text: Send fifty applications tonight to make up for it
options.then: You send them until 2 a.m. and can't remember what you wrote.

steps.why: Saying it to someone you trust keeps the hurt from turning into a verdict.

steps.prompt: A week later, your parents ask what you will do now. What do you say?

options.text: Promise you'll have a job within a month, whatever it takes
options.then: Your father looks relieved, and you feel a new weight settle on you.

options.text: Say you'd rather not talk about it until you feel better
options.then: The conversation ends, and the worry stays in the house unspoken.

options.text: Say you've ruined everything for the family
options.then: Your mother says "Don't say that," but the mood stays heavy.

options.text: Say you're hurt and you're looking at a few options
options.then: Your father nods slowly. "Take your time. Show us the list when it's ready."

steps.why: Naming the hurt and a few options invites support and keeps the talk practical.

steps.prompt: Two weeks on, a senior mentions a short course, an entry-level role and a reattempt route. What do you do?

options.text: Pick the one your relatives would like best
options.then: It sounds impressive at family dinners, and you aren't sure it suits you.

options.text: Note all three and find out what each one needs
options.then: One deadline is close and another is next year, and the picture stops feeling like a wall.

options.text: Wait for the next placement season and do nothing until then
options.then: Months pass quietly, with nothing new to show for them.

options.text: Say you'll think about it and never follow up
options.then: The senior doesn't ask again, and the options go cold.

steps.why: Keeping a few options open shows that a rough season is not the end of the road.

steps.prompt: A month later, a new round opens. The old sting returns as you open the form. What do you do?

options.text: Skip the forms so you don't feel that again
options.then: The month passes without the sting, and without any new chances.

options.text: Apply everywhere without reading what they ask
options.then: You send ten forms and get three polite confusions back.

options.text: Breathe, note one lesson, then apply where it fits
options.then: Your answers are clearer this time, and the form takes one evening.

options.text: Wait until you are sure you'll be selected
options.then: No round ever feels sure, and the deadline passes.

steps.why: Steadying first and choosing by fit beats freezing or applying blindly.

steps.prompt: A classmate asks how placements went for you. What do you say?

options.text: Say you got something great to avoid the questions
options.then: She congratulates you, and you feel the lie sitting between you.

options.text: Say it's over for you and change the subject
options.then: She goes quiet, unsure how to answer.

options.text: Avoid her at lectures for the rest of the week
options.then: She wonders why you've gone quiet, and you feel more alone.

options.text: Say it went badly, and ask how she's doing
options.then: She admits her own season was rough too, and you both feel lighter.

steps.why: Being honest about a hard season, and asking about theirs, reminds you that you aren't alone.

scenarios.debrief: A rough placement season is painful but not final. Support and open options carry you onward.
scenarios.relearn: A bad placement season isn't the end. Lean on support and keep options open.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Kabir has just failed something big and is spiralling.
scenarios.setup: You find him sitting alone on the hostel steps.

steps.prompt: Kabir says: "That's it. I've ruined everything."

options.text: "Don't say that. It's really not that bad."
options.then: He shakes his head. "You don't get it."

options.text: "Yeah, that's pretty bad for you."
options.then: Kabir stares at his shoes. "Right. Thanks."

options.text: "This is a setback, not the end of your story. I'm here."
options.then: He wipes his face. "I don't know what to do."

options.text: "Everyone fails sometimes. Forget it and come for chai."
options.then: He gives a thin smile. "I can't forget it, yaar."

steps.why: A setback isn't the end of someone's story, and saying you're there helps most.

steps.prompt: After a while, he says: "What will everyone think of me?"

options.text: "Who cares what they think? Ignore everyone."
options.then: He shrugs. "Easy for you to say."

options.text: "They'll talk for a few days. You'll have to face it."
options.then: He goes quiet and pulls his knees up.

options.text: "Let me go and explain it to all of them for you."
options.then: He looks alarmed. "No, please don't."

options.text: "One result doesn't decide who you are."
options.then: He nods slowly. "I hope so."

steps.why: One result doesn't change who he is, and friends stay friends.

steps.prompt: Kabir asks: "So what do I even do now?"

options.text: "You should retake it immediately, with no break."
options.then: He winces. "I can't even think about it yet."

options.text: "Honestly, maybe you should change your plans completely."
options.then: He looks startled. "Just like that?"

options.text: "We needn't decide today. One step? I can come to the counsellor with you."
options.then: He breathes out. "Okay. One step. Maybe the counsellor too."

options.text: "Leave it to me. I'll sort it all out for you today."
options.then: He looks relieved for a moment, then uneasy.

steps.why: One small step gives him room, and a counsellor or trusted person can help if it stays heavy.

scenarios.relearn: Remind a struggling friend a setback isn't the end of their story.

scenarios.hook: "Successful people don't fail."

myth.un: Successful people don't fail.
myth.re: Almost everyone successful has a trail of failures behind them; it's part of the path.
myth.why: You only see their wins, not the falls.

scenarios.relearn: Successful people fail plenty; the failures just aren't the part you see.

scenarios.hook: You're so afraid of failing that you avoid trying at all.

steps.prompt: A friend asks you to join her hackathon team. What do you do?

options.text: Say maybe and plan to decide later
options.then: "Later" passes, and the team fills up without you.

options.text: Say no, since it might go badly in front of everyone
options.then: You feel relief, then a small flat feeling.

options.text: Say yes to one small part and see how it goes
options.then: You take the design task, and your hands are cold, but you're in the group chat.

options.text: Say yes to every task so nobody sees you worry
options.then: You take on too much, and the fear grows with each task.

steps.why: A small, real yes lets you try without carrying the whole weight.

steps.prompt: A few weeks later, another chance shows up and the old fear comes with it. What do you do?

options.text: Wait until you feel completely ready
options.then: You wait, and the feeling of ready doesn't arrive.

options.text: Tell a friend you're scared and try a smaller version
options.then: Your friend laughs kindly and says she's scared too, and you start small.

options.text: Try only if you're sure to succeed
options.then: You search for a sure thing, and none of the chances are sure.

options.text: Skip it and tell yourself you didn't want it anyway
options.then: The story sounds fine, and you feel a little smaller.

steps.why: Saying the fear out loud and starting small beats waiting for a guarantee.

steps.prompt: Sooner or later, something you try doesn't go well. What do you do next?

options.text: Take it as a sign you should stop trying
options.then: The old voice gets louder, and avoiding looks safe again.

options.text: Try again tomorrow in the exact same way
options.then: You repeat it and get the same result, more tired than before.

options.text: Write what you learned and one thing to try
options.then: The note is short, and it turns the wobble into a next move.

options.text: Tell no one about it and quietly drop it
options.then: Keeping it hidden adds shame to something ordinary.

steps.why: One note on what you learned turns a miss into something usable.

scenarios.debrief: Avoiding all risk to dodge failure is its own kind of loss, and small brave attempts grow you.
scenarios.relearn: Take small risks. Trying and learning beats never trying.

scenarios.hook: Sort: helps you bounce back, or keeps you down?
scenarios.relearn: Treating failure as feedback, seeking support and planning a small step help you bounce; globalising, isolating and replaying it keep you down.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that are fear talking, not the truth.

scene.text: "This taught me what to change"
"I'm fundamentally not good enough"
"A different route might suit me better"
"One result has decided who I am"
"I can adjust and try again"

scenarios.why: 'Not good enough' and 'one result decided who I am' are fear talking; the others ask what to change and adjust.
scenarios.relearn: A resilient reframe asks what a setback teaches, not whether you're good enough.

scenarios.hook: You did worse than expected and your inner voice is brutal.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice says you always mess up. What do you do?

options.text: Agree with the voice, since it's probably right
options.then: The list of your flaws gets longer with every minute.

options.text: Push the voice down and keep busy all evening
options.then: You stay busy, but the voice returns when the room goes quiet.

options.text: Tell yourself to just think positive and move on
options.then: You say it in the mirror, and it sounds hollow while the hurt stays.

options.text: Ask what you'd say to a friend who got this result
options.then: You picture her face, and your own words start to sound softer.

steps.why: Speaking to yourself as you would to a friend steadies you without pretending it doesn't hurt.

steps.prompt: Later, a friend asks how the result went. What do you say?

options.text: Say it was fine and change the subject quickly
options.then: She believes you, and you're alone with it again.

options.text: List everything you did wrong, step by step
options.then: She listens, but the list grows and so does your low mood.

options.text: Say you hoped for more and you're disappointed
options.then: She says "That's rough," and sits down next to you.

options.text: Joke that you're a total disaster who never learns
options.then: She laughs, then looks unsure whether she should, and the joke cuts a little.

steps.why: Saying plainly that you're disappointed lets someone support you.

steps.prompt: The next test is two weeks away. How do you get ready?

options.text: Study every waking hour to make up for it
options.then: By day five you're exhausted, snapping at people and forgetting things.

options.text: Skip preparing, since another bad result is likely
options.then: You spend two weeks dreading it instead.

options.text: Promise yourself you'll never score this low again
options.then: The promise adds pressure, and every practice question feels like a test of you.

options.text: Find one thing to change and rest properly
options.then: You find one weak topic, fix your plan around it, and sleep through the night.

steps.why: One change plus rest is realistic. Harsh promises only add pressure.

scenarios.debrief: Self-compassion after a setback aids recovery far more than harsh self-criticism.
scenarios.relearn: After a setback, talk to yourself like a struggling friend, not a critic.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: every setback carries a lesson, and bouncing back is a skill you can build. Believe it?
scenarios.affirm: Resilience is learnable; each setback you move through makes the next one more survivable.
scenarios.relearn: Setbacks carry lessons, and bouncing back is a skill you can build.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that are fear talking, not setback-truth.
scenarios.relearn: 'A detour, not a dead end' and 'I can recover' are true; 'ruined' and 'judged forever' are fear talking.

scene.text: "This is a detour, not a dead end"
"My life is ruined"
"I can recover from this"
"Everyone will judge me forever"
"This stings now, but it passes"

scenarios.why: 'Ruined' and 'judged forever' are fear talking; a detour, recovering and 'it passes' are true.

scenarios.hook: After a failure, you want to just give up on the goal entirely.

steps.prompt: You're ready to type a message saying you quit. What do you do?

options.text: Send it so you can't change your mind
options.then: The relief lasts ten minutes. Then you wonder whether you can take it back.

options.text: Ask three friends whether you should quit
options.then: You get three different answers and feel more confused.

options.text: Save it as a draft and rest before deciding
options.then: You put the phone down, and morning feels less final than midnight did.

options.text: Write a long post about how unfair it all was
options.then: It gets a few likes, and the anger stays.

steps.why: A draft keeps the option open while you're too raw to choose.

steps.prompt: A day later, you feel calmer. What do you do next?

options.text: Decide quickly to stay, just to prove you're not a quitter
options.then: You say yes out of pride, and the doubt is still there underneath.

options.text: Drop the goal and try never to think about it again
options.then: The unfinished feeling follows you around.

options.text: Write what happened and what you'd change, then decide
options.then: On paper, the failure looks smaller and more specific.

options.text: Do nothing and hope it sorts itself out
options.then: Days pass, and the decision sits undone.

steps.why: Seeing it on paper separates what happened from what you fear it means.

steps.prompt: You're still unsure a week later. Who do you go to?

options.text: The friend who always says quitting is fine
options.then: He agrees quickly, which is comforting and not very helpful.

options.text: A senior or mentor who has been there
options.then: She shares her own failed attempt, and it helps to hear it isn't unusual.

options.text: A relative who will tell you exactly what to do
options.then: Your uncle gives you a firm plan. It's clear, and it isn't yours.

options.text: No one, since it's your own problem
options.then: You turn it over alone, and it grows in your head.

steps.why: Someone who has been through it helps you choose without taking the decision away.

steps.prompt: Whatever you decide, a relative asks if you're really serious. What do you say?

options.text: Promise you'll never doubt it again
options.then: The promise feels heavy, and you wonder how to keep it.

options.text: Say you were just tired before and it's nothing
options.then: He nods, and you still haven't said what you decided.

options.text: Say what you decided and why, in a calm sentence
options.then: He listens and nods. "Fair enough. Tell me if I can help."

options.text: Change the subject and leave the room
options.then: The question stays in the air for another day.

steps.why: Saying a clear decision calmly, without overpromising, settles the question for you and for them.

scenarios.debrief: Big decisions made in the immediate sting of failure are rarely your best, so rest first.
scenarios.relearn: After a failure, rest before deciding. Don't quit in the heat of it.

scenarios.hook: "Needing more time or another attempt is shameful."

myth.un: Needing more time or another attempt is shameful.
myth.re: Many paths involve a second attempt or a longer route; that's effort, not shame.
myth.why: Persistence is something to respect.

scenarios.relearn: Needing more time or another attempt is persistence, not shame.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the dip you're in now is a chapter, not the whole book. Hold onto that?
scenarios.affirm: This hard chapter is part of a much longer story; it passes, and the book goes on.
scenarios.relearn: A setback is a chapter, not the whole book.

scenarios.hook: "My worth is my marks, package or job title."

myth.un: My worth is my marks, package or job title.
myth.re: Your worth isn't your CV; you are far more than your achievements and status.
myth.why: A person's value was never a number.

scenarios.relearn: Your worth isn't your CV; you're far more than your achievements and status.

scenarios.hook: "A mark sheet is a verdict on who I am."

myth.un: A mark sheet is a verdict on who I am.
myth.re: A result measures one test on one day, not your identity, character or potential.
myth.why: You are not a number on a page.

scenarios.relearn: A mark sheet measures one test, not your identity or potential.

scenarios.hook: Sort: part of your real worth, or just a status marker?
scenarios.relearn: Kindness, character, how you treat people and keeping promises are real worth; package, college 'tier' and impressive titles are status markers.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that value your CV over who you are.

scene.text: "I love who you are"
"Your rank and package are what count"
"How you treat me is what I notice"
"Without the big job, what's there to value"
"You matter to me, results or not"

scenarios.why: The caught lines value a rank, package and job over the person; the people who matter value who you are.
scenarios.relearn: The people who love you value who you are and how you treat them, not your CV.

scenarios.hook: You tie your whole mood to your latest result or offer.

steps.prompt: A result is out and your mood is already swinging with it. What do you do?

options.text: Anchor your worth in who you are, not the score
options.then: You still care about the result. Your sense of self stops moving with it.

options.text: Keep riding every high and low
options.then: Your mood climbs with the number, then drops with the next one.

options.text: Check your rank every hour to be sure of it
options.then: Each refresh gives a short lift, then a longer dip.

options.text: Tell yourself you're nothing without a result
options.then: The thought settles in like a weight, and dims the whole day.

steps.why: Steady worth doesn't rise or fall with a score.

steps.prompt: Friends celebrate their results over chai. What do you do?

options.text: Cheer for them and keep your own worth apart
options.then: You enjoy the chai. Their good day doesn't shrink yours.

options.text: Compare everyone's scores silently in your head
options.then: The chai goes cold while you run the numbers.

options.text: Leave early to avoid the whole thing with them
options.then: Outside, you feel relieved and then lonely.

options.text: Fake excitement about your own result for them
options.then: Your smile stays up for an hour, and then it aches.

steps.why: You can celebrate others without grading yourself.

steps.prompt: The next result is lower than you hoped. What do you do?

options.text: Feel it, learn from it, adjust your next step
options.then: It stings, then turns into a short list of things to change.

options.text: Decide your worth has dropped after this result
options.then: The day turns grey and the thought follows you around.

options.text: Hide the result from everyone you know well
options.then: The secret feels bigger each day you hold it.

options.text: Blame the paper and stop studying for a while
options.then: You feel better for an hour. The next test still comes.

steps.why: A result is information to learn from, not a verdict on you.

scenarios.debrief: Detaching worth from results gets you off an exhausting emotional rollercoaster.
scenarios.relearn: Anchor your worth in who you are, not your latest result.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy source of self-worth, or a fragile one?
scenarios.relearn: Values, relationships, growth, effort and steady self-respect are healthy self-worth; beating others, rank alone and chasing approval are fragile.

scenarios.hook: "A 'settled' high-status job is the only real success."

myth.un: A settled high-status job is the only real success.
myth.re: Success can be a life that fits your values, not just a prestigious title.
myth.why: Prestige and fulfilment aren't the same.

scenarios.relearn: Success can be a life that fits your values, not just a prestigious title.

scenarios.hook: You're tempted to chase a prestigious path you don't actually want, for the status.

steps.prompt: A relative says a famous firm would make the family proud. What do you do?

options.text: Weigh what fits you, not just what impresses others
options.then: You start a short list of what you care about. It feels like your own.

options.text: Chase the status regardless of fit
options.then: You prepare hard. A small voice keeps asking whether you want it.

options.text: Apply just to prove you could get in
options.then: You apply, and feel the pull of proving something to everyone.

options.text: Ask everyone to pick for you, and follow the majority
options.then: The majority says yes, and your own opinion stays unspoken.

steps.why: A path that only impresses others can cost more than it's worth.

steps.prompt: A friend who works at such a firm tells you what a typical week is like. What do you do?

options.text: Listen closely, and compare it with what you care about
options.then: Her week is long and ordinary. You note what you like and what you don't.

options.text: Ignore the details and focus on the name
options.then: You nod along. The name is bright, and the details fade.

options.text: Decide she's just unhappy and ignore it
options.then: It's easy to dismiss her. You learn nothing new.

options.text: Decide you must not be tough enough if it sounds dull
options.then: You turn the dullness into a flaw in yourself.

steps.why: Hearing the real day-to-day shows whether it fits you.

steps.prompt: At dinner your parents ask what you've decided about the big firm. What do you do?

options.text: Explain what fit means to you, and what you're weighing
options.then: They listen, puzzled. "Tell us more about that."

options.text: Say whatever will please them
options.then: They smile. You leave with a promise you aren't sure about.

options.text: Go along quietly and say nothing
options.then: They take your silence for yes, and the path narrows.

options.text: Snap that status doesn't matter at all
options.then: They are hurt, and the real talk is lost.

steps.why: Explaining what fit means to you gives them something to understand.

scenarios.debrief: A prestigious path that doesn't fit you can cost more than it's worth; fit matters.
scenarios.relearn: Choose for fit and values, not just status that impresses others.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: you were a whole, worthy person long before any job or result. Still are. Feel it?
scenarios.affirm: Your worth came before any achievement and stays whatever happens with your career.
scenarios.relearn: You're a whole, worthy person independent of any job or result.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two beliefs that make worth something you have to achieve.

scene.text: "My worth is steady, whatever my results"
"I'm only worth as much as I achieve"
"I matter beyond my output"
"Stop achieving and I stop mattering"
"I'm enough as I am, off the scoreboard"

scenarios.why: The caught beliefs make worth conditional on achievement; steady worth is unconditional, not earned by output.
scenarios.relearn: Your worth is steady and beyond your output, not earned by achievement alone.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Kabir was rejected for a job he wanted badly.
scenarios.setup: Tonight he sits beside you, staring at his phone.

steps.prompt: Kabir says: "They said no. I guess I'm just not good enough."

options.text: "One no isn't a measure of you. I'm here."
options.then: He exhales. "It feels like all of me got rejected."

options.text: "Don't think like that. Just think positive!"
options.then: He shrugs. "Easy for you to say."

options.text: "Maybe the interviewers saw something real."
options.then: He stares at the floor. "That's what I'm afraid of."

options.text: "Everyone gets rejected. You'll be fine tomorrow."
options.then: He nods, unconvinced. "I don't think I will be."

steps.why: A rejection is one outcome, not a measure of the person, and he needs to hear that first.

steps.prompt: Kabir says: "I keep replaying the interview. What did I do wrong?"

options.text: "Replay it all night. You'll find the mistake."
options.then: He nods grimly. "Right. I'll go through every answer."

options.text: "Nothing. They were just unfair to you."
options.then: He looks up, unsure. "Then why does it hurt this much?"

options.text: "Stop thinking about it. Forget the whole thing."
options.then: He tries to smile. "I wish I could switch it off."

options.text: "Let's note one thing to try next time, then stop."
options.then: He writes a line in his phone. "Okay. Just one."

steps.why: Picking one thing to adjust turns replaying into learning, then rest.

steps.prompt: A week later Kabir says: "Everyone's posting offers. Should I even apply again?"

options.text: "Only apply where they'll definitely want you."
options.then: He frowns. "Nobody can promise that."

options.text: "Wait until you feel completely sure."
options.then: He nods. "Sure." The feeling doesn't come, and the week passes.

options.text: "Yes. Try one this week, and I'll sit with you."
options.then: He half smiles. "One. Okay. You're on."

options.text: "Take a year off and forget about jobs."
options.then: He looks relieved, then uneasy. "A whole year?"

steps.why: One small application, with a friend beside him, moves him forward without pressure.

scenarios.hook: Your aunt Sunita only seems proud of you when your results are good.
scenarios.setup: Tonight she calls to ask how your exams went.

steps.prompt: Aunt Sunita says: "Tell me your marks. I want to be proud of you."

options.text: "They're good. I'll make you proud. Don't worry."
options.then: She beams. The promise sits in your chest like a debt.

options.text: "Why do you only care about marks?"
options.then: Her voice sharpens. "I'm only asking out of love."

options.text: "Ask me after the results are out, Aunty."
options.then: She sighs. "Fine. Call me that very day."

options.text: "I'm working hard. My worth isn't only marks, Aunty."
options.then: She pauses. "Hmm. Well, I do know you work hard."

steps.why: You can be warm and steady: your worth isn't only your results.

steps.prompt: Aunt Sunita says: "Your cousin topped his college. What about you?"

options.text: "Maybe I'm just not as good as him."
options.then: She clicks her tongue. "Don't say that." The doubt stays.

options.text: "He always gets the attention. I don't care."
options.then: "Why so bitter?" she says, and the call turns cold.

options.text: "I'm glad for him. I'm doing my own best, Aunty."
options.then: "Hmm." A pause. "Well, that's a fair answer."

options.text: "I'll top next time. I promise."
options.then: She smiles. "That's more like it." The bar just went up.

steps.why: You can be glad for him and still hold your own steady worth.

steps.prompt: Later your mother says: "Aunty means well. What will you tell her at Diwali?"

options.text: "Can you talk to her for me, please?"
options.then: She hesitates. "It would sound better from you."

options.text: "I know she does. I'd like to be seen for more than marks."
options.then: Your mother softens. "Then tell her that. Kindly, the way you just told me."

options.text: "Fine. I'll just tell her what she wants."
options.then: She nods, relieved. You feel the old bar settle again.

options.text: "She'll never change. Forget it."
options.then: Your mother frowns. "You can't say that about family."

steps.why: Saying what you want plainly, without a fight, keeps you both close and true.

scenarios.relearn: Keep your worth steady, even when others tie pride to results.

steps.prompt: A senior on the impressive route says it drains them. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself they're just tired and ignore it

scenarios.hook: You want to write to someone in a field you're curious about.
scenarios.setup: You have her profile open, and a blank message box.

steps.prompt: Your friend Sana says: "She's on the company page. What will you write?"

options.text: "Can you get me a job at your firm, please?"
options.then: Sana winces. "That's a big ask for a first message."

options.text: "Can I send you my CV for feedback?"
options.then: Sana tilts her head. "She doesn't know you yet. Start with why you're curious."

options.text: "I'm exploring your field. How did you start?"
options.then: Sana nods. "That's easy to say yes to. Send it."

options.text: "She won't bother with someone like me, honestly."
options.then: Sana frowns. "You don't know that. You haven't asked."

steps.why: A curious, simple message makes it easy for her to say yes.

steps.prompt: Sana says: "What if she ignores you?"

options.text: "I won't send it, so she can't ignore me."
options.then: Sana sighs. "Then you'll never know, will you?"

options.text: "Then I'll try someone else. A no is data."
options.then: Sana grins. "Exactly. Keep your list of people going."

options.text: "Then I'll know I'm not worth her time."
options.then: Sana shakes her head. "Busy people miss messages all the time."

options.text: "I'll message her five more times."
options.then: Sana winces. "That's a fast way to get blocked."

steps.why: A silence is not a verdict. It just means trying someone else too.

steps.prompt: Sana says: "Say she agrees to a call. What will you ask her?"

options.text: "How did you start? What would you redo?"
options.then: Sana smiles. "Those are real questions. She'll enjoy answering."

options.text: "Can you get me a job?"
options.then: Sana shakes her head. "She'll feel cornered. Ask for advice."

options.text: "Nothing. I'll just listen."
options.then: Sana raises her eyebrows. "She'll wait. A question helps her help you."

options.text: "What's your salary, and is it worth it?"
options.then: Sana winces. "That's pretty direct for a first call."

steps.why: Asking about her path and what she'd do differently gets you guidance, not just facts.

scenarios.relearn: A simple, curious outreach can open a door, even without a network.

scenarios.hook: You feel paralysed trying to make the perfect choice.

steps.prompt: Two options sit in front of you and the form closes in a week. What do you do?

options.text: Keep researching until one feels certain
options.then: Seven days of tabs open. On the last day, you pick in a rush.

options.text: Ask everyone you know until they agree
options.then: Everyone says something different. You pick at the deadline, still unsure.

options.text: Pick the safer one just to be done
options.then: You submit fast, then wonder whether relief was the only reason.

options.text: Pick the best current fit and adjust later

steps.prompt: A month in, something about the choice doesn't fit. What do you do?

options.text: Ignore it, since changing means you chose wrong

options.text: Drop everything and restart from zero

options.text: Decide you ruined it and feel stuck

options.text: "That sounds heavy. No one has it figured out."

options.text: "Just try harder, yaar. You'll get there soon."

options.text: "Stop feeling sorry for yourself, yaar. Come on."

steps.prompt: Kabir says: "People say it gets better, but I can't see how."

options.text: "It just does. Trust me. It always does, somehow."

options.text: "Then stop comparing and just try to stay positive."

options.text: "Maybe you should rethink your whole plan, then."

steps.prompt: Kabir says: "Some nights I can't sleep because of it."

options.text: "That's a lot to carry. Want to find support together?"

options.text: "Everyone has sleepless nights. Just ignore it, okay?"

options.text: "Try a motivational podcast tonight. It might help."

options.text: "Have some more coffee and work it all out tonight."

steps.prompt: A few days later Kabir asks: "Who would I even talk to about all this?"

options.text: "Just talk to me. Nobody else needs to know."

myth.un: I should have bounced back by now; still hurting means I'm weak.
myth.re: Recovery isn't a deadline; feeling it for a while is part of healing, not weakness.
myth.why: Resilience includes letting it hurt first.

scenarios.relearn: Taking time to feel a setback is part of recovery, not weakness.

scenarios.hook: "If I really had talent, I wouldn't have struggled like this."

myth.un: If I really had talent, I wouldn't have struggled like this.
myth.re: Struggle is how skill is built, not proof it's missing; even strong people hit walls and work through them.
myth.why: Difficulty isn't a verdict on ability.

scenarios.relearn: Struggling with something hard builds skill; it doesn't prove you lack it.

scenarios.hook: "Failing in front of everyone means I can never show my face."

myth.un: Failing in front of everyone means I can never show my face.
myth.re: People remember a public stumble far less than you fear; most are too busy with their own worries.
myth.why: The spotlight feels bigger than it is.

scenarios.relearn: A public setback fades fast for everyone but you; you can show up again.

scenarios.hook: "I have to get it right the first time or not bother."

myth.un: I have to get it right the first time or not bother.
myth.re: Almost nothing worthwhile is got right first try; iterating is the normal way things actually work.
myth.why: First drafts are meant to be rough.

scenarios.relearn: Getting it wrong first and iterating is the normal route, not a failure.

scenarios.hook: "Getting laid off in my first job means I'm unhireable."

myth.un: Getting laid off in my first job means I'm unhireable.
myth.re: Layoffs are usually about budgets and timing, not your worth; plenty of strong people get caught in them.
myth.why: A layoff isn't a performance verdict.

scenarios.relearn: A layoff is rarely about you; it doesn't make you unhireable.

scenarios.hook: "I switched my branch, so I clearly couldn't handle the first one."

myth.un: I switched my branch, so I clearly couldn't handle the first one.
myth.re: Switching toward a better fit is a smart pivot, not a defeat; choosing what suits you is strength.
myth.why: Pivots are legitimate routes, not retreats.

scenarios.relearn: Switching to a better-fit branch is a pivot, not proof you couldn't cope.

scenarios.hook: "Everyone in my batch got placed except me, so something's wrong with me."

myth.un: Everyone in my batch got placed except me, so something's wrong with me.
myth.re: Placement timing varies hugely; many strong people land roles off-campus or months later.
myth.why: A slower start isn't a flaw in you.

scenarios.relearn: Getting placed later than your batch is timing, not something wrong with you.

scenarios.hook: "I bombed the interview, so I should give up on that field."

myth.un: I bombed the interview, so I should give up on that field.
myth.re: One rough interview is a skill you can practise, not a closed door; the next one can go differently.
myth.why: Interviewing improves with reps.

scenarios.relearn: A bad interview is a skill to practise, not a reason to quit the field.

scenarios.hook: "I failed once, so I'll obviously fail every time I try again."

myth.un: I failed once, so I'll obviously fail every time I try again.
myth.re: A past result doesn't decide the next one; you carry what you learned into the next attempt.
myth.why: Each attempt starts fresh, wiser.

scenarios.relearn: One failure doesn't predict the next; you go in having learned.

scenarios.hook: Your results are out and far below what you hoped.

steps.prompt: Your phone is buzzing with messages. What do you do tonight?

options.text: Decide tonight that you're done with the field
options.then: By midnight the decision feels final, even though nothing has been tested.

options.text: Let yourself feel it and look at options tomorrow
options.then: You cry a little, eat something and sleep, and the options will still be there tomorrow.

options.text: Scroll to see everyone else's results
options.then: You find scores higher than yours, and your stomach drops.

options.text: Plan a reattempt until morning
options.then: You plan until 3 a.m. and feel more wired than sure.

steps.why: The first hour of bad news is a poor time to write the whole verdict.

steps.prompt: Next morning, your mother asks how you are. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're fine and there's nothing to discuss
options.then: She looks unconvinced and watches you closely all day.

options.text: Say you'll do whatever the family decides
options.then: She relaxes, but now the decision sits in other people's hands.

options.text: Say you're upset and need a day before planning
options.then: She squeezes your hand. "Okay. Eat something first."

options.text: Say you've let everyone down
options.then: She says "No, no," but the words hang in the room.

steps.why: Asking for a day is honest and gives everyone room to think calmly.

steps.prompt: Two days later, you sit down with the result and a cup of chai. What do you do?

options.text: Put it in a drawer and stay away from it for now
options.then: The result sits in the drawer and keeps tugging at you.

options.text: Choose the first option a relative suggests to you
options.then: It's a relief to have an answer, but it isn't one you've weighed.

options.text: Read only the lowest marks again and again tonight
options.then: Each re-read sharpens the sting and tells you nothing new.

options.text: List what worked, what didn't and two options
options.then: The list is short, and the next step looks smaller than the night before.

steps.why: A short, honest list turns a raw result into choices you can weigh.

scenarios.debrief: Disappointment is real, but don't let the raw first hour write the verdict.
scenarios.relearn: Feel a bad result first, then weigh next steps once the sting settles.

scenarios.hook: You missed the cutoff for the course you wanted by a few marks.

steps.prompt: The list is out and your name is just below the line. What do you do?

options.text: Decide only that one course could ever work for you
options.then: You close every other tab, and the room feels very small.

options.text: Ask a relative about a "contact" who can get you in
options.then: The conversation leaves you uneasy, and nothing is certain.

options.text: Look up the next-best courses and the reattempt dates
options.then: You find three courses close to your interests and a date for next year.

options.text: Wait for seats to open and do nothing else
options.then: You refresh the list every day, and nothing else moves forward.

steps.why: Checking close fits and dates keeps your options real.

steps.prompt: A cousin tells you to just retry and forget every other route. What do you say?

options.text: Agree right away so you don't have to think
options.then: The matter feels settled, and you haven't looked at anything else.

options.text: Say retrying is pointless
options.then: He raises an eyebrow, and the talk turns into an argument.

options.text: Say you'll compare the reattempt with other routes first
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay, but don't take too long."

options.text: Say you'll decide after seeing what all your batchmates do
options.then: You watch your batch for weeks, and their paths don't match yours.

steps.why: Comparing routes by what fits you is sturdier than following one piece of advice.

steps.prompt: A teacher sets out three courses that still have seats, and the forms close next week. How do you choose?

options.text: Pick the one with the most impressive name
options.then: It impresses people at functions, and you've not checked if it suits you.

options.text: Pick whichever your friends are joining
options.then: You'll have company, but the course may not match your interests.

options.text: Talk to someone in each course, then choose by fit
options.then: A student in one course describes a typical week, and it sounds like you.

options.text: Wait until the last day and choose in a rush
options.then: The rush leaves you choosing on nerves alone.

steps.why: Someone in the course can tell you what it's really like, and fit matters more than a name.

steps.prompt: A month later, a classmate on your new course asks why you're there. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's only a backup, so you won't really try here
options.then: She nods, and you feel half in and half out of the room.

options.text: Complain about the college that turned you down
options.then: She listens, and the talk leaves you both tense.

options.text: Say you missed a cutoff and you're giving this a fair try
options.then: She smiles. "Same here, honestly. It's better than I thought."

options.text: Say you chose it on purpose from the start
options.then: She nods, and you feel the small lie sitting there.

steps.why: Saying it plainly, without apology, lets you settle into the path you chose.

scenarios.debrief: A near-miss is painful, but it is rarely the only door, and nearby fits often work out.
scenarios.relearn: Missing one cutoff leaves real options. Explore close fits and reattempts.

scenarios.hook: A scholarship you counted on got rejected.

steps.prompt: The email says only "not selected." What do you do first?

options.text: Decide you don't deserve any funding at all
options.then: The thought hangs over the evening, and the fees feel even bigger.

options.text: Hide the money worry from your whole family
options.then: You carry it alone, working out fees late at night.

options.text: Reapply tomorrow without changing anything
options.then: You send the same form, and nothing in it is different.

options.text: Write and ask what was missing for next time
options.then: A short reply comes within days and points out two gaps.

steps.why: Asking what was missing turns one no into information.

steps.prompt: You're short on fees, and the college office has a notice board of options. What do you do?

options.text: Borrow from a moneylender to cover it quickly
options.then: The money arrives fast, and the interest grows faster.

options.text: Wait and hope the fee deadline gets extended
options.then: The deadline stays, and the worry grows.

options.text: Skip the notice board since others probably took those options
options.then: The board still has three open options you never see.

options.text: Ask the office about other scholarships and instalments
options.then: The clerk shows you two schemes and a way to pay in parts.

steps.why: The office knows the options, and asking costs nothing.

steps.prompt: Two new scholarship forms are open, and one needs an essay. What do you do?

options.text: Apply only to the one without an essay
options.then: It takes an hour, and the stronger option goes unused.

options.text: Send one generic application to both
options.then: The forms are quick to fill, and neither sounds like you.

options.text: Skip both, since you've already been turned down once
options.then: The deadlines pass, and you wonder what might have happened.

options.text: Start both, and tailor each one to its scheme
options.then: The essay takes two evenings, and the second form reuses much of it.

steps.why: Tailoring each form to its scheme raises your chances without starting from zero.

steps.prompt: Next term, a new scholarship with an essay opens, and a senior offers to show you hers. What do you do?

options.text: Decline, since asking feels like cheating
options.then: You write alone, and the draft stays stuck on its first paragraph.

options.text: Copy lines from her essay into yours
options.then: The essay reads well, and it doesn't sound like you.

options.text: Thank her and say you'll ask later
options.then: Later never comes, and the deadline gets closer.

options.text: Read her essay, then ask for feedback
options.then: She circles two sentences and suggests how to make them yours.

steps.why: Learning from someone who has done it is a normal, smart way to grow your own application.

scenarios.debrief: Funding is competitive, and one no is feedback for the next try, not a judgement on you.
scenarios.relearn: A scholarship no is feedback to refine and reapply, not a verdict on your worth.

scenarios.hook: You made a visible mistake on a team project and feel like quitting.

steps.prompt: Your teammates have just seen the error in your part of the slides. What do you do?

options.text: Blame the unclear instructions
options.then: Your teammates go quiet, and the error still needs fixing.

options.text: Stay silent and hope someone else fixes it
options.then: Two days pass and the error is still there.

options.text: Apologise again and again and offer to redo the whole project
options.then: They tell you it's too much, and the mood gets awkward.

options.text: Say "That's my mistake" and offer to fix it
options.then: One teammate nods. "Thanks. Send the new version by tonight."

steps.why: Owning it plainly and fixing it is what teammates remember.

steps.prompt: The next group meeting is tomorrow. How do you show up?

options.text: Skip it and say you're feeling unwell
options.then: The group carries on, and your absence is what they notice.

options.text: Show up, share the fix and ask for more
options.then: They assign you the charts, and the meeting moves on quickly.

options.text: Come but sit quietly and avoid speaking
options.then: You feel invisible, and the group wonders if you're still in.

options.text: Come with a new plan for the whole project
options.then: Nobody asked for a new plan, and the group is unsure how to respond.

steps.why: Showing up with the fix rebuilds standing faster than hiding.

steps.prompt: Before the final, a teammate says the mistake cost the group time. What do you say?

options.text: Say everyone makes mistakes and you'd rather not talk about it
options.then: She frowns. "It's not about blame. It just cost us time."

options.text: Say it wasn't only you, since the instructions weren't clear
options.then: She sighs, and the talk turns into an argument about who is at fault.

options.text: Say maybe you should just leave the group
options.then: She looks uncomfortable. "I didn't say that."

options.text: Say "You're right" and explain what you changed to avoid it again
options.then: She nods. "Okay. That works for me."

steps.why: Saying what you changed rebuilds trust better than defending or hiding.

steps.prompt: The project is done and the group plans a short debrief. What do you do?

options.text: Say nothing and hope the mistake is forgotten
options.then: The debrief ends, and the slip hangs unspoken.

options.text: Skip it and say you've got other work to do
options.then: They move on without you and you never learn what they thought.

options.text: Bring the mistake up and apologise again at length
options.then: The debrief becomes about you, and the group is unsure how to respond.

options.text: Say what you learned and thank the group
options.then: Someone smiles. "We all learned something. Good project."

steps.why: A short, honest note on what you learned closes the loop for everyone.

scenarios.debrief: A mistake handled openly is forgotten fast, and teammates remember how you recovered.
scenarios.relearn: After a visible mistake, own it and keep contributing rather than withdraw.

scenarios.hook: You've been rejected from several jobs in a row.

steps.prompt: Another rejection email comes in. What do you do?

options.text: Decide you're simply not employable
options.then: The thought sits heavy, and the next application feels pointless.

options.text: Apply to twice as many places without changing anything
options.then: You send twenty forms, and the replies sound much the same.

options.text: Go through your applications and look for a pattern
options.then: You notice most of your applications lack the same detail.

options.text: Stop checking your email for a few weeks
options.then: The weeks pass quietly, and no new chances come in.

steps.why: A pattern in the rejections shows you what you can actually change.

steps.prompt: An older friend who hires people at work offers to read your CV. What do you do?

options.text: Rewrite the whole CV with fancier words
options.then: The CV sounds impressive and less like you.
