options.text: Say it's fine and you don't want to bother her
options.then: She shrugs, and the CV goes out unread by anyone else.

options.text: Hand it over, then argue with every comment she makes
options.then: She stops offering feedback halfway through.

options.text: Hand it over and ask for honest feedback
options.then: She points out two missing details and a long paragraph nobody reads.

steps.why: Honest feedback on a CV is one of the fastest ways to fix a pattern.

steps.prompt: A week later, a posting comes up that fits you well. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for a posting that feels perfect
options.then: You wait, and two good ones close unseen.

options.text: Send your usual CV because it's faster
options.then: The form goes in quickly, and the old gaps are still there.

options.text: Tailor your CV to this posting, and keep applying
options.then: The form takes an hour, and it reads sharper than before.

options.text: Apply, then message the recruiter every day
options.then: The recruiter's replies get shorter each day.

steps.why: A tailored application, plus other options open, turns the streak into a strategy.

steps.prompt: At an interview, they ask how your search has been going. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's been smooth and you've had many offers
options.then: The interviewer raises an eyebrow, and you feel the gap.

options.text: Say you'll take any job at all
options.then: The interviewer smiles politely, and the talk moves on without warmth.

options.text: Say it's been tough, and you've been learning from it
options.then: He nods. "That's a useful thing to know about yourself."

options.text: Say you've been rejected by everyone and it's unfair
options.then: The room feels heavy, and the interview turns defensive.

steps.why: Saying what you've learned shows resilience without hiding the hard part.

steps.prompt: After the interview, you wait a week for a reply. What do you do?

options.text: Call every day until you get an answer
options.then: The calls irritate the office, and no answer comes sooner.

options.text: Send one polite follow-up and keep applying
options.then: You get a short reply saying a decision comes next week.

options.text: Wait without doing anything else
options.then: The week stretches, and nothing else moves forward.

options.text: Assume it's a no and stop looking
options.then: You stop looking, and a good posting passes unseen.

steps.why: One polite follow-up plus other applications keeps you moving without leaning on one answer.

scenarios.debrief: A rejection streak usually points to something adjustable, not to your worth.
scenarios.relearn: A run of rejections is a signal to adjust your approach, not proof you're unemployable.

scenarios.hook: Your family is disappointed about your low marks, and the room feels heavy.

steps.prompt: Your father says quietly that they expected more. What do you do?

options.text: Promise you'll top the next exam, whatever it takes
options.then: He nods, and you feel the weight of the promise.

options.text: Say nothing and go to your room for a while
options.then: The house stays tense until dinner.

options.text: Say you've let everyone down
options.then: Your mother says "No, beta," and the talk goes round in circles.

options.text: Say it's a dip and you have a plan
options.then: He looks up. "Tell us. We're listening."

steps.why: Naming the dip and a small plan moves the room from blame to next steps.

steps.prompt: At dinner, your mother asks what you plan to do now. What do you say?

options.text: Say you'll do whatever they tell you to do about it
options.then: She sighs, and the plan stays in other people's hands.

options.text: Say marks don't matter at all to you anymore
options.then: Your father goes quiet, and the worry is left unanswered.

options.text: Share two steps: a study group and asking your teacher
options.then: She nods. "Those sound reasonable. Start this week."

options.text: Say you don't know and stop talking about it
options.then: The table goes quiet, and nobody knows how to help.

steps.why: Two small, specific steps make the worry practical instead of personal.

steps.prompt: A week later, your cousin posts her high score on the family group. How do you respond?

options.text: Mute the group, then keep checking her score anyway
options.then: The group is silent, and you still open it to look at her marks.

options.text: Compare your score with hers again and again
options.then: The evening goes by in numbers that don't help.

options.text: Send her a warm congratulations and get back to studying
options.then: She replies with a heart, and you get an hour of study done.

options.text: Post a past achievement of yours to show you're fine
options.then: A few relatives like it, and it feels a little hollow.

steps.why: Congratulating her and getting on with your own work stops her score from becoming a verdict on you.

scenarios.debrief: Family worry is real, but a calm next step does more than a verdict on yourself.
scenarios.relearn: After a dip, name a small plan rather than absorb it as proof you've failed.

scenarios.hook: You froze and went blank during a big presentation.

steps.prompt: Back in your seat, your face is hot and the moment replays. What do you do?

options.text: Decide you're simply bad at speaking in front of people
options.then: The thought feels final, and the next talk already seems impossible.

options.text: Replay it until you've found every single mistake
options.then: The list gets long, and your mood drops with it.

options.text: Pretend it didn't happen and avoid your classmates
options.then: The avoiding makes the silence louder.

options.text: Note what triggered the freeze, such as the first slide
options.then: You write "first slide, too many eyes," and it feels less mysterious.

steps.why: Noticing the trigger turns a freeze into something you can train.

steps.prompt: Your teacher offers a short retake next week. What do you do?

options.text: Say no, since it's better to let it go
options.then: The marks stay as they are, and so does the fear.

options.text: Say yes, then plan to memorise every word
options.then: The script feels safe and gets stiff as you practise.

options.text: Say yes and practise out loud with a friend
options.then: By the second run, your first two minutes flow.

options.text: Say you'll decide on the last possible day
options.then: The last day comes, and the decision is made in a rush.

steps.why: Practising out loud with someone is a small, doable way to train for the moment.

steps.prompt: The next time you have to present, your heart races as you stand up. What do you do?

options.text: Rush through it so it's over quickly
options.then: You finish fast and feel you didn't say what you meant.

options.text: Read every word from the slides
options.then: You finish, though your eyes never reach the room.

options.text: Apologise to the class for last time before you begin
options.then: The apology fills the start, and your nerves grow.

options.text: Take one slow breath and begin with your first line
options.then: Your voice shakes, then settles by the third sentence.

steps.why: One slow breath and a practised first line give the nerves somewhere to land.

scenarios.debrief: Freezing under pressure is common and trainable, not a verdict on speaking.
scenarios.relearn: A presentation freeze is something to prepare for, not a reason to stop speaking up.

scenarios.hook: You failed your driving test and feel humiliated.

steps.prompt: The examiner hands you the slip. What do you do when you get home?

options.text: Tell yourself you're just bad at everything you try
options.then: The thought spreads to things that have nothing to do with driving.

options.text: Read the feedback and book a couple more lessons
options.then: The slip lists two turns to practise, and the lessons are booked.

options.text: Rebook the test for tomorrow without extra practice
options.then: The earliest slot is a week away, and nothing has changed by then.

options.text: Tell nobody and stay away from the car for a while
options.then: The silence makes the failure feel larger than it is.

steps.why: The slip shows what to practise, so a few lessons can fix what went wrong.

steps.prompt: At a family function, a cousin who heard about it laughs that he passed first time. What do you say?

options.text: Snap that driving is stupid anyway
options.then: He laughs again, and the mood turns sour.

options.text: Go quiet and feel small for the rest of the function
options.then: You leave early, and the ache comes with you.

options.text: Say you'll pass with a better score than his
options.then: The conversation becomes a contest you didn't plan.

options.text: Laugh a little and say you're working on it
options.then: He shrugs. "Fair. Tell me when you pass."

steps.why: A light, honest answer lets the comment pass without becoming a contest.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, your retest is close, and one kind of turn still makes you nervous. What do you do?

options.text: Skip practice and hope the examiner doesn't ask for it
options.then: The turn comes up, and your hands freeze.

options.text: Book extra lessons on everything except that turn
options.then: You are more confident overall, and the turn is still the weak point.

options.text: Book a lesson just for that turn
options.then: After a few tries, the turn feels smoother.

options.text: Cancel the retest until you feel completely confident
options.then: The weeks pass, and the confidence doesn't arrive.

steps.why: Practising the exact weak spot fixes it faster than general preparation.

scenarios.debrief: Small fails feel huge in the moment, but most just need a bit more practice.
scenarios.relearn: Failing a small test means practise and retry, not "I'm bad at everything."

scenarios.hook: A senior gave you harsh feedback and you want to shut down.

steps.prompt: Her comments on your report are blunt and stinging. What do you do first?

options.text: Decide you're hopeless and stop working on it
options.then: The report sits untouched, and the deadline gets closer.

options.text: Reply with a list of what's wrong with her comments
options.then: She replies shortly, and the talk turns into a quarrel.

options.text: Fix everything she mentioned right away without thinking
options.then: You change twelve things, and lose what worked.

options.text: Take a break, then reread for what's useful
options.then: With a calmer head, two comments stand out as fair.

steps.why: A pause lets you find the useful part without the sting.

steps.prompt: One of her comments isn't clear to you. What do you do?

options.text: Guess what she meant and change it
options.then: Your guess misses, and the section gets worse.

options.text: Skip that comment, since asking might look weak
options.then: The comment stays unresolved, and the section is still unclear.

options.text: Ask a friend to guess what she meant
options.then: He shrugs and offers a guess that doesn't quite fit.

options.text: Ask her to explain with an example
options.then: She sends a two-line example, and it makes sense.

steps.why: Asking for an example clears up the comment, and asking for help is a smart move.

steps.prompt: You send the revised report. She replies with one more suggestion. What do you do?

options.text: Feel the sting again and ignore it
options.then: The suggestion stays in your inbox, unread by your brain.

options.text: Reply defending your choices at length
options.then: She doesn't answer, and the thread goes cold.

options.text: Accept it but stop asking her anything from now on
options.then: The next report has questions she could have answered.

options.text: Thank her and work the suggestion in
options.then: The new version reads cleaner, and she sends back a short "Better."

steps.why: Taking the useful part, leaving the tone, is how harsh feedback helps you grow.

steps.prompt: A month later, she asks you to help a junior with a similar report. What do you do?

options.text: Say no, since you're not good enough to help
options.then: She seems surprised and finds someone else.

options.text: Say yes, and give the junior the same blunt tone
options.then: The junior gets quiet, and her report doesn't improve.

options.text: Say yes but only send a file, without talking to her
options.then: The file helps a little, and the junior still has questions.

options.text: Say yes and share how you handled the sting
options.then: The junior relaxes and starts asking questions.

steps.why: Sharing what helped, and how you handled the sting, turns feedback into support for others.

scenarios.debrief: Harsh feedback often hides a useful signal, so take the lesson and drop the delivery.
scenarios.relearn: Harsh feedback has a usable part. Keep that and adjust rather than shut down.

scenarios.hook: You failed a paper you actually studied hard for.

steps.prompt: The result is in and you studied for weeks. What do you do?

options.text: Decide studying is pointless since it failed
options.then: The thought spreads, and the books stay shut.

options.text: Study twice as long next time with the same method
options.then: You add hours, and the tiredness adds up with them.

options.text: Blame the paper setter and leave it there
options.then: The anger feels fair, and nothing you can change is left.

options.text: Go through the paper and compare it with your method
options.then: You see you only re-read notes and never practised questions.

steps.why: Comparing the paper with your method shows what can change.

steps.prompt: A topper in your class offers to share how she prepares. What do you do?

options.text: Copy her whole timetable exactly
options.then: Her timetable doesn't fit your day, and you drop it within a week.

options.text: Say thanks, but you're not like her
options.then: The offer ends, and so does the chance to learn.

options.text: Ask about her method and try one part of it
options.then: You try her practice-question habit for a week, and it already feels different.

options.text: Decline since you don't like asking for help
options.then: You go on alone, and the method stays the same.

steps.why: Trying one part of a method is easier than copying a whole routine.

steps.prompt: The retest is in three weeks. How do you start?

options.text: Go back to only re-reading your notes all day
options.then: The notes feel familiar, and the gaps are still there.

options.text: Try five new methods all at the same time
options.then: By day four, you've stopped all of them.

options.text: Wait a week for the motivation to arrive
options.then: The week passes, and the retest is now two weeks away.

options.text: Practise past questions and review each mistake
options.then: The first set shows which topics to fix.

steps.why: Practising questions and reviewing mistakes shows where the method is working.

scenarios.debrief: When effort doesn't land, the method is often what to tweak, not your worth.
scenarios.relearn: If hard study didn't pay off, examine the method rather than give up on studying.

scenarios.hook: You're tempted to hide your reattempt year from everyone.

steps.prompt: A close school friend in another city messages to ask what you're up to. What do you do?

options.text: Say you're busy with a few things these days
options.then: She replies "Nice!" and the chat ends.

options.text: Invent an internship so you sound busy and sorted
options.then: She asks for details, and you have to keep track of the story.

options.text: Mute the chat and say nothing about it at all
options.then: She sends another message, and the silence feels awkward.

options.text: Tell her it's a reattempt year and ask about hers
options.then: She replies "That takes guts. I had a tough year too."

steps.why: Sharing it plainly with a friend you trust turns hiding into a normal chat.

steps.prompt: Apart from your parents, hardly anyone else knows, and it feels heavy. What do you do?

options.text: Tell everyone at once on the family group
options.then: The replies come in fast, and you're not sure which ones to answer.

options.text: Tell the relative who'll judge you most, to get it over with
options.then: He frowns, and the talk leaves you drained.

options.text: Tell one trusted person, such as a cousin or mentor
options.then: She listens and smiles. "I'm glad you told me."

options.text: Keep hiding and avoid gatherings
options.then: The gatherings pass, and so do the small chances to feel understood.

steps.why: One trusted person can carry part of the weight without the pressure of everyone knowing.

steps.prompt: A function is coming up, and everyone will ask about your year. What do you do?

options.text: Skip the function and stay home that day
options.then: The day passes quietly, and the questions are waiting for next time.

options.text: Plan a story about a fake job at a company
options.then: The story gets longer each time someone asks.

options.text: Prepare a long explanation to justify your year
options.then: The explanation sounds defensive, and you feel tense.

options.text: Choose a short, calm line and keep the talk light
options.then: "I'm preparing again, and it's going well" lands easily, and the talk moves on.

steps.why: A short, calm line means you decide how much to share.

scenarios.debrief: Reattempts are common and nothing to hide, and sharing usually meets understanding.
scenarios.relearn: A reattempt is normal. Sharing it with someone you trust beats carrying it in secret.

scenarios.hook: After one rejection you're about to delete the whole application draft.

steps.prompt: Your cursor is on Delete All. What do you do?

options.text: Delete it all to make a clean start
options.then: The page goes blank, and only an old copy in your email survives.

options.text: Edit it angrily and send it straight out
options.then: You change things in a rush and create new errors.

options.text: Save it in a folder and close the file
options.then: The folder holds your work, and the evening feels lighter.

options.text: Keep the file but never open it again
options.then: The draft sits untouched, and so does the lesson in it.

steps.why: Saving the draft keeps the work you put in, and you can return to it calmly.

steps.prompt: A few days later, another round opens. What do you do?

options.text: Start from a blank page to avoid the old memory
options.then: The blank page takes a whole weekend to fill again.

options.text: Open the old draft and mark what to update
options.then: You find two weak answers, and the rest stands.

options.text: Send the draft unchanged
options.then: The same gaps go out again.

options.text: Wait for a round that feels like a sure thing
options.then: No round ever feels like a sure thing, and this one closes.

steps.why: Reusing the draft and updating what's weak is faster than starting over.

steps.prompt: Working on the next application, you find one weak answer. What do you do?

options.text: Delete the whole section and start again
options.then: The section takes hours to rewrite from nothing.

options.text: Leave it, since it's probably fine
options.then: The answer goes in as it is.

options.text: Rewrite just that answer and get it read
options.then: A friend reads it, and her two comments sharpen it in twenty minutes.

options.text: Rewrite every answer to sound more impressive
options.then: The whole application loses its own voice.

steps.why: Fixing the one weak answer keeps what works and uses a second pair of eyes.

scenarios.debrief: Frustration tempts you to torch your work, but most of it is reusable next time.
scenarios.relearn: After a rejection, keep your work. The next attempt builds on it, not from scratch.

scenarios.hook: You compare your failure to a friend's smooth run and feel worthless.

steps.prompt: Your friend posts about getting a placement right away. What do you do?

options.text: Take it as proof that you're the failure
options.then: The thought lingers, and the day feels heavier.

options.text: Screenshot his post and compare it with your own record
options.then: You line them up, and the gap looks larger than it is.

options.text: Unfriend him so you don't see it again
options.then: The feed gets quieter, and so does the friendship.

options.text: Remind yourself you only see his highlights
options.then: You think about what he isn't posting, and the sting eases.

steps.why: You see his edited version, not everything he went through.

steps.prompt: A few days later, you meet him in the canteen. What do you do?

options.text: Talk only about his news and hide yours for now
options.then: He thinks you're fine, and you feel more alone.

options.text: Mention your setback to make him feel guilty about it
options.then: He looks uncomfortable, and the conversation ends early.

options.text: Avoid him so you don't feel worse about yourself
options.then: You skip lunch to dodge him, and the day is lonely.

options.text: Ask how he's really been, and share how you've been
options.then: He admits the interviews made him anxious too, and you both relax.

steps.why: An honest chat reminds you that both of you are working through it.

steps.prompt: You sit down to plan your next step. What do you use as your yardstick?

options.text: His timeline, as posted on his profile
options.then: You try to copy his dates, and they don't fit your life.

options.text: The average timeline of everyone in your batch
options.then: The average hides how different each person's situation is.

options.text: What would impress your relatives at functions
options.then: The plan looks good at family functions, and it doesn't match you.

options.text: Your own last month and what you learned from it
options.then: The list gives you two steps that feel realistic.

steps.why: Your own progress is the fair measure, because it's the only one that's about you.

scenarios.debrief: You're comparing your raw moment to their edited one, which is not a fair scoreboard.
scenarios.relearn: A setback compared to someone's highlight reel isn't a fair measure of you.

scenarios.hook: A long-term goal fell through and you feel directionless.

steps.prompt: It's Sunday and you have nothing planned. What do you do?

options.text: Wait until you feel motivated again to start
options.then: The day passes, and so does the feeling of being ready.

options.text: Plan the next five years in detail tonight
options.then: The plan fills a page, and it feels impossible by morning.

options.text: Pick one tiny step, like sending one email
options.then: The email takes ten minutes, and the week gets a handle.

options.text: Sleep in and scroll your phone all day
options.then: The day disappears, and the heaviness is still there.

steps.why: One tiny step gives you a handle without needing the full map.

steps.prompt: Midweek, a friend asks what's next for you. What do you say?

options.text: Say you have a full plan
options.then: He nods, and you feel the pressure of the plan you don't have.

options.text: Say you don't know and change the subject
options.then: He backs off, and you've shared nothing.

options.text: Say whatever the family expects
options.then: He nods, and you wonder if that's really what you want.

options.text: Say you're trying small things and exploring
options.then: He grins. "Same. Let's compare notes sometime."

steps.why: Honest exploring is easier to say, and easier to keep doing.

steps.prompt: A workshop on something you're curious about is open for sign-up. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it because it isn't part of the old plan
options.then: The sign-up closes, and the curiosity stays.

options.text: Sign up only if it will look good on your CV
options.then: You're more interested in how it looks than what you'd learn.

options.text: Wait for a sign that it's the right thing
options.then: No sign arrives, and the registration closes.

options.text: Sign up, since it matches your interest
options.then: The first session surprises you, and you leave with two new ideas.

steps.why: Following your interest gives direction without needing the whole map.

scenarios.debrief: After a goal collapses, a small concrete step does more than waiting to feel ready.
scenarios.relearn: When a goal falls through, one small next step beats waiting for motivation.

scenarios.hook: You keep replaying one mistake from months ago.

steps.prompt: It's 2 a.m. and the scene is playing again. What do you do?

options.text: Replay it once more to make sure you've punished yourself enough
options.then: The loop tightens, and sleep gets further away.

options.text: Scroll your phone to drown it out
options.then: The screen fills the silence, and the thought waits behind it.

options.text: Tell yourself to stop thinking about it, right now
options.then: The harder you push, the louder it gets.

options.text: Write what the mistake taught you in one line
options.then: The line is short, and the scene feels a little smaller.

steps.why: A one-line lesson lets the memory do its job and then rest.

steps.prompt: The next day, the memory shows up again during class. What do you do?

options.text: Follow the memory and dig into every detail
options.then: You miss ten minutes of the lecture.

options.text: Leave class to be alone
options.then: The hall is quiet, and so is your mind for a while.

options.text: Tell the whole story to whoever sits beside you
options.then: She listens, and the telling makes it feel bigger.

options.text: Notice it, name it, and go back to class
options.then: The thought passes by, and you catch the next slide.

steps.why: Naming the loop lets it pass without taking over your day.

steps.prompt: A friend says she does the same thing with an old mistake. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's silly to dwell on the past
options.then: She looks away, and the topic closes.

options.text: Agree that some mistakes can't be forgiven
options.then: She looks sadder than before.

options.text: Swap stories and replay yours in full detail
options.then: You both end up more upset than when you began.

options.text: Suggest jotting down the lesson, and ask about hers
options.then: She smiles. "I'll try that tonight."

steps.why: Sharing a way to capture the lesson helps both of you let the loop rest.

scenarios.debrief: Rumination keeps the pain without the learning, so capture the lesson and let it rest.
scenarios.relearn: Once a mistake's lesson is learned, replaying it only punishes. Let the loop close.

scenarios.hook: A bad result has hit you hard.

steps.prompt: Two weeks on, the heaviness is still there most days. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself to tough it out alone
options.then: The weight stays, and so does the quiet.

options.text: Wait until after the next exam to see if it lifts
options.then: The exam comes and goes, and the heaviness stays.

options.text: Keep busy with extra classes so you don't notice
options.then: You're tired by evening, and the feeling is waiting.

options.text: Reach out to a counsellor or call Tele-MANAS 14416
options.then: You make the call, and saying it out loud feels strange and a little lighter.

steps.why: Reaching out is smart, and a heavy feeling after a setback is never your fault.

steps.prompt: A friend notices and asks if you're okay. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're just tired from the exams
options.then: She nods, and the heaviness stays where it was.

options.text: Say you're fine and change the subject
options.then: She watches you a little longer before going back to her notes.

options.text: Say you'll tell her after the exam is over
options.then: The exam comes, and you still haven't said it.

options.text: Say it's been heavy and you want help
options.then: She sits with you and says she's glad you told her.

steps.why: Saying it to someone you trust lets them support you.

steps.prompt: Dr. Mehta, the campus counsellor, has a slot open this week. What do you do?

options.text: Decline, since counsellors are for bigger problems
options.then: The slot goes to someone else, and the heaviness stays.

options.text: Take it, but plan to say everything is fine
options.then: You sit in the room, and the talk stays on the surface.

options.text: Say you'll come only if it gets worse
options.then: The week passes, and you don't come.

options.text: Take the slot, even if you don't know what to say
options.then: She says that's common, and asks you to start anywhere.

steps.why: Going without knowing what to say is enough, and it's never a sign of failing.

steps.prompt: A few weeks later, the heaviness has eased and then a bad night comes back. What do you do?

options.text: Decide nothing will help, since it came back
options.then: The thought is loud tonight. It is only a thought, and support is still a call away.

options.text: Hide it so they don't think you've slipped back
options.then: The silence makes the night heavier.

options.text: Promise yourself you'll ask next time instead of tonight
options.then: The night passes alone, and the promise rests on tomorrow.

options.text: Call Tele-MANAS 14416 or a friend and say it's come back
options.then: A calm voice listens and stays on the line with you.

steps.why: A bad night coming back is never your fault. Reaching out when it does is steady recovery.

scenarios.debrief: When a setback tips into constant heaviness, support is the strong move: Tele-MANAS 14416, or someone you trust.
scenarios.relearn: When hopelessness lingers, reaching out for support is strength, not weakness.

scenarios.hook: Sort: setback as information, or setback as a verdict?

items.text: "This shows me what to study differently"
"I can ask where I went wrong"
"This is one data point to adjust on"
"This is who I am, full stop"

scenarios.relearn: Lines that ask what to adjust treat a setback as information; lines that decide who you are treat it as a verdict.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy way to cope with a setback, or an unhealthy one?

items.text: Talking it through with a friend
Numbing it by doomscrolling all night
Breaking the comeback into small steps
Pretending you don't care at all
Avoiding anything linked to it forever

scenarios.relearn: Talking it out, small steps and resting then planning are healthy; numbing, pretending and avoiding forever are not.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a real next step after a setback, or a trap that keeps you stuck?

items.text: Asking a mentor for one tip
Listing what you'd change next time

scenarios.relearn: Booking practice, asking for a tip and listing changes move you; waiting to feel ready, comparing and 'it's hopeless' keep you stuck.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a kind thing to tell yourself after a setback, or a harsh one?

items.text: "That was hard; I'm allowed to feel it"
"I can try again when I'm steadier"
"One bad day isn't the whole me"

scenarios.relearn: Allowing the feeling, planning a retry and 'one bad day isn't all of me' are kind; 'always ruin everything' and 'I deserve this' are harsh.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a fact about failure that's true, or a myth?

items.text: One failure decides your whole life
Needing a second attempt is shameful

scenarios.relearn: That most succeeders failed first, resilience is learnable and pivots are normal is true; the rest are myths.

scenarios.hook: Sort: which line keeps a door open, and which slams it shut?
scenarios.relearn: 'I can reapply', 'other routes exist' and 'I can ask' keep doors open; 'never another chance', 'this or nothing' and 'no point asking' slam them shut.

scenarios.hook: A classmate named Nisha just got a low result and is crying.
scenarios.setup: You sit down beside her in the corridor.

steps.prompt: Nisha says, through tears: "I studied so hard. What's wrong with me?"

options.text: "You really should have studied more, na."
options.then: She flinches and turns away.

options.text: "Stop crying. Everyone is watching."
options.then: She wipes her eyes quickly and goes silent.

options.text: "This is one result, not the whole of you. I'm here."
options.then: She leans her head on her knees. "Thanks."

options.text: "Nothing's wrong with you. Let's go out and forget it."
options.then: She shakes her head. "I can't forget it yet."

steps.why: A result is one day's work, and feeling heard comes before fixing it.

steps.prompt: Nisha says: "My parents will be so upset."

options.text: "They'll be fine. Don't worry about it."
options.then: She sniffs. "You don't know my parents."

options.text: "Just hide the result for now."
options.then: She looks uneasy. "That'll make it worse later."

options.text: "They may be worried. Want to plan what to say?"
options.then: She nods. "Maybe something simple."

options.text: "I'll call them and explain it all for you."
options.then: She looks startled. "No, please. I should do it."

steps.why: Planning what to say lets her face them herself without being alone.

steps.prompt: Nisha asks: "Do you think I'm not cut out for this?"

options.text: "Maybe. Not everyone is meant for this course."
options.then: She stares at you. "Wow. Okay."

options.text: "Of course you are. You're the smartest person here."
options.then: She gives a thin smile. "You're just being nice."

options.text: "One paper can't say that. Let's look at it together."
options.then: She opens her bag and takes out the paper.

options.text: "You can't know yet, so let's not think about it."
options.then: She sighs. "It's all I can think about."

steps.why: One paper can't tell her that, and looking at it together turns it into information.

steps.prompt: Nisha says: "I think I want to ask the teacher what happened."

options.text: "Don't bother. Teachers never change anything."
options.then: Her shoulders drop. "Then what's the point?"

options.text: "Ask later, when it's less embarrassing."
options.then: She nods. "Okay. Maybe next week."

options.text: "Sounds good. I can wait outside if you like."
options.then: She smiles faintly. "I'd like that."

options.text: "I'll ask them for you. You stay here."
options.then: She shrugs. "If you're sure."

steps.why: Asking the teacher is a real next step, and company makes it easier to take.

scenarios.relearn: Remind someone a single result isn't the whole of them, and offer to look at a next step.

scenarios.hook: Your inner critic is loud after you messed up at work.
scenarios.setup: You're at your desk, replaying the mistake.

steps.prompt: Your inner critic says: "You're useless and everyone can see it."

options.text: "You're right. I always do this kind of thing."
options.then: The voice answers: "See? I told you so."

options.text: "I made a mistake. I'm not a mistake. I'll fix it."
options.then: The voice pauses. "Fine. But you'll never live it down."

options.text: "Stop it. I'm not listening to you anymore today."
options.then: The voice goes quiet for a minute, then returns louder.

options.text: "Maybe I can work all night and make up for it."
options.then: The voice answers: "You'll be too tired to do it well."

steps.why: Separating the mistake from yourself lets you fix it without the extra weight.

steps.prompt: Your inner critic says: "Everyone at work is judging you now."

options.text: "They probably are. I should stay out of sight."
options.then: The voice says, "Good luck hiding in a small office."

options.text: "I'll go and apologise to every one of them."
options.then: The voice answers: "That'll take all morning."

options.text: "Some may have noticed. Most are busy."
options.then: The voice mutters, "Maybe."

options.text: "I'll be perfect from tomorrow so they forget."
options.then: The voice laughs. "Perfect? You?"

steps.why: Most people are busy with their own work, and being perfect isn't the goal.

steps.prompt: Your inner critic says: "What if you mess up again?"

options.text: "Then I'm done. I might as well quit."
options.then: The voice grows louder, and fixing the mistake feels further away.

options.text: "Don't think about that. I'll check everything for hours."
options.then: The voice answers: "That's a lot of hours."

options.text: "I'll just avoid anything that could go wrong."
options.then: The voice says, "Then you'll do very little."

options.text: "Then I'll fix it again, and ask for help sooner."
options.then: The voice goes quiet for a while.

steps.why: Fixing it and asking for help sooner is how people work well, and it isn't a weakness.

scenarios.relearn: Speak to yourself after a slip the way you'd steady a friend, not a critic.

scenarios.hook: You're in a reattempt year, and Sunita Aunty has opinions about it.
scenarios.setup: It's a family gathering, and other relatives are listening.

steps.prompt: Sunita Aunty says: "A year lost is a year lost, beta. You're behind now."

options.text: "Yeah, you're right. I've messed up my life."
options.then: She nods and sighs. "Well, we will see what can be done."

options.text: "Aunty, that's rude. Please stop commenting on my life."
options.then: The room goes silent. "I only said it because I care."

options.text: "Hm. Has anyone tried the samosas yet?"
options.then: She takes it as agreement and tells the next person.

options.text: "I see it differently. This is me taking another route."
options.then: She frowns. "Route? Everyone your age is moving ahead."

steps.why: Saying it calmly marks your path as your own without starting a fight.

steps.prompt: She says: "And what will you do if it doesn't work out this time?"

options.text: "It has to work. I can't afford to fail again."
options.then: She looks satisfied, and your chest tightens.

options.text: "I don't know. I can't think about that."
options.then: She shakes her head. "That's the problem, beta."

options.text: "Then I'll look at the other routes I've already noted."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "You've noted them?"

options.text: "Then I'll do whatever the family thinks is right."
options.then: She smiles. "Good. That's the sensible way."

steps.why: Having other routes in mind shows you have a plan, and you don't have to promise success.

steps.prompt: Your uncle adds: "Even the Kapoors' son cleared it in one go, no?"

options.text: "Everyone is better than me, I know."
options.then: He chuckles. "Well, at least you admit it."

options.text: "Then why don't you ask him for help?"
options.then: He bristles. "I was only saying."

options.text: "I'll show all of you by topping it this time."
options.then: He nods. "That's the spirit."

options.text: "Good for him. I'm going at my own pace."
options.then: He shrugs. "Hmm. Fair."

steps.why: Being glad for someone and going at your own pace keeps the comparison from becoming a verdict.

steps.prompt: Later, your mother asks softly: "Did those comments bother you?"

options.text: "No, it's fine. I'm just tired from the day."
options.then: She studies your face but lets it go.

options.text: "They were right. I'm letting you all down."
options.then: She holds your hand. "No, beta. That's not true."

options.text: "Yes. Maybe I should stop coming to these gatherings."
options.then: She sighs. "They're family, beta. But I understand."

options.text: "A little. Can we talk about how I'm doing?"
options.then: She nods. "Yes. Tell me how you really are."

steps.why: Telling her it stung, and asking for her support, lets her stand with you.

scenarios.relearn: You can gently hold that a reattempt is a route, not falling behind.

scenarios.hook: Your junior Tarun is too scared of failing to even try.
scenarios.setup: He stands at the notice board reading about the club tryouts.

steps.prompt: Tarun says: "What if I mess it up in front of everyone?"

options.text: "Yeah, maybe don't risk it, just in case."
options.then: He nods, relieved, but keeps looking at the poster.

options.text: "You won't mess up. You're too good for that."
options.then: He frowns. "You can't know that."

options.text: "Trying beats not trying. You'll learn something."
options.then: He thinks. "I guess that's true."

options.text: "Just don't be scared. It's really not hard."
options.then: He sighs. "That doesn't work."

steps.why: Trying teaches him something even if it goes badly, and skipping teaches nothing.

steps.prompt: Tarun asks: "What if I try and I'm just bad at it?"

options.text: "Then everyone will see it. Better to skip."
options.then: His face falls. "Yeah. Maybe."

options.text: "Then we'll practise every day until you're perfect."
options.then: He looks worried. "Perfect? That's even more pressure."

options.text: "You won't be. Stop doubting yourself."
options.then: He shrugs. "Easy to say."

options.text: "Then you'll have a first try to learn from."
options.then: He laughs a little. "Okay, that's fair."

steps.why: A first try is how almost everyone starts, and it gives him something to learn from.

steps.prompt: Tarun asks: "If I did try, what would I even do first?"

options.text: "Just go in and do the hardest part first."
options.then: He pales. "That sounds terrifying."

options.text: "Wait until you feel completely ready."
options.then: He nods. "I'll wait, then."

options.text: "Think about it for another month or two."
options.then: He sighs. "The tryouts will be over by then."

options.text: "Pick one small step. I'll come with you."
options.then: He smiles. "Okay. Sign-up tonight."

steps.why: A small first step, plus company, makes it doable.

scenarios.relearn: Encourage someone that trying and learning beats avoiding the risk entirely.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Zara has just been turned down for something she really wanted.
scenarios.setup: You're at the canteen, and she's staring at her phone.

steps.prompt: Zara says: "I'm done. They said no. What's the point?"

options.text: "Don't be dramatic. It's just one rejection."
options.then: She stiffens. "It's not just one to me."

options.text: "You're right. Some things aren't meant to be."
options.then: She nods slowly and looks even sadder.

options.text: "It's okay that it hurts. One no isn't the end."
options.then: She lets out a breath. "It really hurts."

options.text: "Let's go out and not think about it at all."
options.then: She shakes her head. "I can't stop thinking about it."

steps.why: Saying it hurts first, and that one no isn't the end, lets her feel heard.

steps.prompt: Zara says: "I worked so hard on this. It feels pointless."

options.text: "Hard work doesn't really matter anyway."
options.then: She looks at you, shocked. "Then why try at all?"

options.text: "You just have to keep thinking positive."
options.then: She rolls her eyes. "That's not helping."

options.text: "Your work wasn't wasted. It carries over."
options.then: She looks up. "You think so?"

options.text: "Maybe you should have worked a bit harder."
options.then: She pushes her chair back. "Wow."

steps.why: Her work carries forward, so it isn't wasted.

steps.prompt: Zara says: "Everyone else seems to get in on the first go."

options.text: "True, everyone else is ahead right now."
options.then: She slumps. "Yeah."

options.text: "Don't compare. Just be happy for them."
options.then: She frowns. "I'm trying."

options.text: "Then let's find out who they are and copy them."
options.then: She laughs weakly. "That's not going to help."

options.text: "We only see their wins, not their no's."
options.then: She tilts her head. "Really?"

steps.why: We only see others' wins, and most people have a few no's behind them.

steps.prompt: Zara asks: "What do I even do next?"

options.text: "Apply to ten places tonight and forget this one."
options.then: She winces. "I can't do ten tonight."

options.text: "Wait a few months and see how you feel."
options.then: She nods, but looks unsure.

options.text: "Do whatever your parents say."
options.then: She sighs. "They'll just say to try again."

options.text: "Let's look at one next step together. A counsellor can help too."
options.then: She opens her laptop. "Okay. One. Maybe I'll talk to someone too."

steps.why: One small step together keeps her moving, and a counsellor can help if it stays heavy.

scenarios.relearn: Validate the hurt first, then reframe one rejection as not the end.

scenarios.hook: You bump into a classmate right after a public flop.
scenarios.setup: It's the corridor outside the auditorium.

steps.prompt: Your classmate Imran says: "Hey. That didn't go great, did it?"

options.text: "I'm such a joke. Everyone must be laughing at me."
options.then: He looks uncomfortable. "No, not everyone."

options.text: "It went fine, actually. Others messed up far more than me."
options.then: He raises his eyebrows. "Okay. If you say so."

options.text: "I can't talk right now. Sorry, I have to go."
options.then: He nods, then calls after you. "Wait. Can I ask one thing?"

options.text: "That didn't go how I wanted. I'll figure out what's next."
options.then: He nods. "Fair. Most people would be rattled."

steps.why: Naming it plainly and pointing to a next step keeps the flop from defining you.

steps.prompt: Imran says: "What do you think went wrong?"

options.text: "Everything. I'm just bad at this."
options.then: He frowns. "That can't be true."

options.text: "The judges didn't like me from the start."
options.then: He shrugs. "Maybe."

options.text: "I rushed the middle. I'll slow it down."
options.then: He nods. "That's a fixable thing."

options.text: "Nothing went wrong. The mic was bad."
options.then: He smiles politely and lets it go.

steps.why: Naming one specific fix turns a flop into something you can work on.

steps.prompt: Imran says: "A few of us are heading for chai. Come along?"

options.text: "No. I don't want anyone to see me."
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay. Another day."

options.text: "I'll come, but only if nobody talks about it."
options.then: He nods. "Sure."

options.text: "Sure, and I'll joke about how bad I was all evening."
options.then: He chuckles, though it's a bit awkward.

options.text: "Sure. I'd like the company."
options.then: He grins. "Come on, then."

steps.why: Choosing company after a flop keeps you connected instead of hiding.

scenarios.relearn: You can name a flop plainly and point to a next step, without collapsing into shame.

scenarios.hook: Your teammate Ravi is spiralling after his part of the project failed.
scenarios.setup: He's slumped in the lab after the demo.

steps.prompt: Ravi says: "My part broke in front of everyone. I ruined the whole thing."

options.text: "Well, you did kind of sink the whole thing."
options.then: He covers his face with his hands.

options.text: "It's not your fault at all. It was everyone's fault."
options.then: He shakes his head. "That's not true either."

options.text: "This part flopped, not you. Let's see what it taught us."
options.then: He lowers his hands. "Okay. I'm listening."

options.text: "Forget it. Let's not talk about the demo."
options.then: He slumps further. "I can't just forget it."

steps.why: A failed part is not the same as a failed person, and looking at what it taught helps.

steps.prompt: Ravi says: "They'll never trust me with anything again."

options.text: "They probably won't. Stay in the background for a while."
options.then: He nods glumly. "Yeah."

options.text: "They don't care. Don't think about it."
options.then: He shakes his head. "They care."

options.text: "I'll tell them it was my code that broke."
options.then: He looks uneasy. "But it wasn't."

options.text: "They'll remember how you handle this."
options.then: He sits up a little. "Okay. Then I'll fix it properly."

steps.why: People remember how someone handles a failure more than the failure itself.

steps.prompt: Ravi asks: "Where do I even start fixing it?"

options.text: "Rewrite the whole thing tonight, every line."
options.then: He groans. "That'll take days."

options.text: "Leave it for whoever takes over from you next."
options.then: He looks away. "That doesn't feel right."

options.text: "Ask the professor for an extension before anything."
options.then: He nods. "Maybe. But that doesn't fix it."

options.text: "Let's list what failed and fix the smallest piece."
options.then: He opens his laptop. "Okay, the login bug."

steps.why: A short list and the smallest piece first make the job feel possible.

steps.prompt: Ravi says: "I feel like quitting the team."

options.text: "Fine. Quit, and we'll manage without you."
options.then: He looks stung. "Oh. Okay."

options.text: "You can't quit now. We all need you here."
options.then: He sighs. "Now I feel worse."

options.text: "Decide right now so the team knows."
options.then: He frowns. "I can't do that."

options.text: "Take a night to rest. We'll look tomorrow."
options.then: He nods slowly. "Okay. Tomorrow."

steps.why: Deciding after rest is wiser than deciding in the sting of a failure.

scenarios.relearn: Separate a failed task from the person, and offer to learn from it together.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that pile shame on instead of helping you bounce back.

scene.text: "Let's see what I can adjust next time"
"I always ruin everything I touch"
"It's okay to feel low about this"
"Everyone was right to doubt me"
"I can ask someone for a hand"

scenarios.why: 'I always ruin everything' and 'everyone was right to doubt me' globalise and shame; the others adjust and ask for help.
scenarios.relearn: A bounce-back response adjusts and asks for help, not globalise a slip into shame.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two responses to a rejection that keep you stuck.

scene.text: "I'll ask for feedback and reapply"
"I'll never put myself out there again"
"This stings, but it's survivable"
"This proves I'm just not good enough"
"Let me try a slightly different angle"

scenarios.why: 'Never again' and 'not good enough' keep you stuck; the others ask for feedback, call it survivable and try a new angle.
scenarios.relearn: A healthy reaction to rejection asks for feedback and retries, not quits.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two 'comfort' lines that actually dismiss the person.

scene.text: "That sounds really hard; I'm here"
"Just stay positive, it's nothing"
"Want to figure out a next step together?"
"Others have it way worse than you"
"It's okay to feel low right now"

scenarios.why: 'Just stay positive' and 'others have it worse' dismiss the feeling; the others validate it and offer support.
scenarios.relearn: Real comfort validates the feeling and offers support, not dismisses it.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two beliefs about failure that simply aren't true.

scene.text: "Resilience is a skill I can build"
"You either have grit or you don't"
"Most people pivot at some point"
"One failure marks you for life"
"Setbacks can redirect me to a better fit"

scenarios.why: 'You either have grit or you don't' and 'one failure marks you for life' are myths; the others are true.
scenarios.relearn: Resilience is learnable and pivots are normal; one failure doesn't mark you for life.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that turn a setback into a permanent verdict.

scene.text: "This tells me what to change"
"This is just who I am now"
"I can recover from this"
"There's no coming back from this"
"This is one chapter, not the book"

scenarios.why: 'Just who I am now' and 'no coming back' make a setback permanent; the others treat it as changeable and recoverable.
scenarios.relearn: A setback is information you can act on, not a permanent verdict on who you are.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two reactions to a bad result that aren't healthy coping.

scene.text: "I'll talk to someone I trust"
"I'll just numb out and avoid it all"
"I'll rest, then make a small plan"
"I'll catastrophise the whole future"
"I'll treat this as feedback"

scenarios.why: Numbing/avoiding and catastrophising aren't healthy coping; the others talk it out, rest then plan, and take feedback.
scenarios.relearn: Healthy coping talks it out, rests and plans, and takes feedback, not numbs out.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a setback is information about what to adjust, not a verdict on who you are. Sit with that?
scenarios.affirm: A setback points at what to change next; it never gets to decide who you are.
scenarios.relearn: A setback is information to adjust on, not a verdict on who you are.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: failure is a comma in your story, not a full stop. How does that sit?
scenarios.affirm: A setback punctuates the sentence; the story keeps going and you keep writing it.
scenarios.relearn: Failure is a comma in your story, not a full stop.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: almost everyone you admire has a trail of failures you never see. Believe it?
scenarios.affirm: The people who look sorted fell plenty too; you just never saw that part.
scenarios.relearn: Almost everyone you admire failed along the way; you only see the wins.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: it's allowed to feel a setback fully before you bounce. Give yourself that?
scenarios.affirm: Feeling it first isn't weakness; it's the part that lets the bounce actually hold.
scenarios.relearn: It's okay to feel a setback fully before bouncing back; there's no rush.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the version of you a year from now will have moved well past today's setback. Picture them?
scenarios.affirm: From a year out, today's setback is a small mark on a long road you kept walking.
scenarios.relearn: A year on, today's setback will look much smaller; you keep moving.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a second attempt isn't a sign you failed. It's just persistence. Take that in?
scenarios.affirm: Going again is effort and persistence, the very thing that gets people where they're going.
scenarios.relearn: A second attempt is persistence, not a sign you've failed.

scenarios.hook: Match each setback to the steadying truth that meets it.
scenarios.relearn: Each setback has a true, steadying response: failures redirect, are common, are survivable and don't define you.

pairs.right: "It often redirects to a better fit"
"One no isn't a verdict on me"

scenarios.hook: Match the unhelpful thought to its resilient reframe.
scenarios.relearn: Each catastrophic thought has a resilient reframe that treats the setback as workable, not final.

pairs.right: "This is a detour, not a dead end"
"It's a comma, not a full stop"

scenarios.hook: Match each part of bouncing back to what it looks like in practice.
scenarios.relearn: Bouncing back means feeling it, learning from it, taking a step, leaning on support and being kind to yourself.

pairs.right: Let yourself be low for a bit
Ask what you'd change next time
Book one small action this week
Talk to you like a friend

scenarios.hook: Match each setback myth to the truth that corrects it.
scenarios.relearn: Common failure myths each have a correcting truth: failure is normal, learnable to recover from, and not a verdict.

scenarios.hook: Match each feeling after a setback to a healthy next move.
scenarios.relearn: Each tough feeling after a setback has a healthy next move, from resting to reaching for support.

scenarios.hook: Match each thing a setback can give you to what it teaches.
scenarios.relearn: A setback can teach direction, method, resilience, humility and what you actually value.

pairs.right: You can get through hard things

scenarios.hook: Match each persona's setback to the route that fits them.
scenarios.relearn: Different people meet a setback with different fitting next steps, from off-campus routes to gentle pushback.

pairs.right: Find a mentor or campus service

scenarios.hook: Match each unhelpful coping habit to a healthier swap.
scenarios.relearn: Each numbing or avoiding habit has a healthier swap that actually helps you recover.

pairs.right: A short walk and early sleep
One small step back toward it

scenarios.hook: "My batchmate already has a job offer, so I've clearly fallen behind."

myth.un: My batchmate has an offer, so I've fallen behind.
myth.re: One person's timeline isn't your deadline; your path runs at its own pace, not theirs.
myth.why: Different people land at different times; nobody's clock sets yours.

scenarios.relearn: One person's offer isn't your deadline; your path runs at its own pace.

scenarios.hook: "Everyone on LinkedIn is celebrating, so they must all be doing great."

myth.un: Everyone on LinkedIn is doing great.
myth.re: LinkedIn shows posted wins, not the rejections, gaps and worry people leave off their feed.
myth.why: People share offers and promotions, not the silence between them.

scenarios.relearn: LinkedIn shows posted wins, not the rejections and gaps people leave out.

scenarios.hook: "My cousin cracked it in one attempt, so something must be wrong with me."

myth.un: My cousin cracked it first try, so I'm flawed.
myth.re: You're comparing your full struggle to a single clean line from their story you never saw inside.
myth.why: You only saw their result, never the doubts behind it.

scenarios.relearn: You're comparing your whole struggle to one clean line of someone else's story.

scenarios.hook: "If I keep watching toppers' day-in-my-life reels, I'll get motivated too."

myth.un: Watching toppers' reels will motivate me.
myth.re: Those edited reels mostly leave you feeling behind; your own small next step actually moves you.
myth.why: Feeling inadequate drains energy; it rarely fuels real action.

scenarios.relearn: Edited toppers' reels mostly leave you behind; your own next step moves you.

scenarios.hook: "My whole batch seems sorted; I must be the only one quietly panicking."

myth.un: I'm the only one quietly panicking.
myth.re: Most of your batch is feeling behind too; the calm faces are hiding the same worry you are.
myth.why: Outer confidence usually covers private doubt.

scenarios.relearn: Most of your batch feels behind too; calm faces often hide the same worry.

scenarios.hook: "Their startup got funded and I'm nowhere, so my work doesn't count."

myth.un: Their funding means my work doesn't count.
myth.re: Their win takes nothing from you; your progress is real whether or not anyone announced it.
myth.why: Someone else's headline isn't a verdict on your effort.

scenarios.relearn: Their win takes nothing from you; your progress is real, announced or not.

scenarios.hook: "She's already engaged and settled; clearly I'm late at everything."

myth.un: She's settled, so I'm late at everything.
myth.re: There's no shared schedule everyone's on; 'late' is measured against a standard you invented.
myth.why: Lives unfold on different timelines, not one fixed one.

scenarios.relearn: There's no shared schedule; 'late' is measured against a standard you invented.

scenarios.hook: "Checking who got placed every hour keeps me sharp and ready."

myth.un: Refreshing the placement list keeps me sharp.
myth.re: Hourly checking mostly spikes anxiety; stepping back and doing your own prep helps far more.
myth.why: Constant comparison rattles you; focused work steadies you.

scenarios.relearn: Hourly placement-checking spikes anxiety; your own prep helps far more.

scenarios.hook: "He's posting from abroad while I'm stuck here, so he's just better than me."

myth.un: He's abroad, so he's just better than me.
myth.re: A photo from abroad is one frame, not a ranking of two lives; his post says nothing about your worth.
myth.why: A travel photo is a moment, not a measure of a person.

scenarios.relearn: A photo from abroad is one frame, not a ranking of two whole lives.

scenarios.hook: "Everyone seems to know exactly what they want; I'm clearly behind for not knowing."

myth.un: Everyone knows what they want, so I'm behind.
myth.re: Most confident-looking people are figuring it out as they go; not-knowing-yet is a normal place to stand.
myth.why: Certainty is often performed, not felt.

scenarios.relearn: Most confident people are figuring it out too; not-knowing-yet is normal.

scenarios.hook: "My friend's salary is double mine, so I clearly made the wrong choices."

myth.un: Their bigger salary means I chose wrong.
myth.re: A number on one payslip can't judge a whole path; fit and what matters to you aren't on that figure.
myth.why: A pay figure measures one job, not your direction or worth.

scenarios.relearn: A salary figure can't judge a whole path; fit isn't on a payslip.

scenarios.hook: "My roommate studies less and scores more, so I'm just not smart enough."

myth.un: They study less and score more, so I'm not smart.
myth.re: You see their result, not their method, background or off-screen effort; this isn't a fair head-to-head.
myth.why: You compare your visible struggle to their visible outcome only.

scenarios.relearn: You see their result, not their method; it's never a fair head-to-head.

scenarios.hook: "If I'm not as far along as my school friends, I've wasted these years."

myth.un: Behind my school friends means I wasted these years.
myth.re: You've grown in ways no scoreboard shows; 'behind' assumes one finish line that doesn't exist.
myth.why: Growth isn't only the milestones others post.

scenarios.relearn: You've grown in ways no scoreboard shows; there's no single finish line.

scenarios.hook: "Their highlight reel proves they never struggle the way I do."

myth.un: Their highlight reel proves they never struggle.
myth.re: A highlight reel is the edit, not the footage; the cut-out doubts and bad days are there, just unposted.
myth.why: People share the best take, not the bloopers.

scenarios.relearn: A highlight reel is the edit; the bad days are there, just unposted.

scenarios.hook: Sort: the edited highlight reel, or the unposted real picture?

items.text: The convocation photo with the gold medal
The four years of late-night doubt before it
The eleven rejection mails not screenshotted
The argument and burnout behind that launch

scenarios.relearn: The medal and caption are the reel; the doubt and rejections are the real picture.

scenarios.hook: Sort: eases the comparison spiral, or feeds it?

items.text: Muting accounts that make you feel small
Talking honestly with a friend who gets it
Counting who posted an offer this week
Reading the comments to see who's ahead

scenarios.relearn: Muting triggers, honest talk and tracking your own progress ease the spiral; rival-stalking and offer-counting feed it.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a fair comparison, or a rigged one?

items.text: You today vs you at the start of the year
Your day one vs their year five
Your effort vs the goals you set
Your raw reality vs their posted highlights
Your progress vs your own last attempt
Your behind-the-scenes vs their final cut

scenarios.relearn: Measuring against your past self and your goals is fair; against their year five or their final cut is rigged.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a kind, true thought, or a comparison distortion?

items.text: "Everyone my age is ahead of me"

scenarios.relearn: 'My own pace' and 'their wins don't shrink mine' are true; 'everyone's ahead' and 'I'm failing' are distortions.

scenarios.hook: Sort: helps your headspace, or fuels the comparison ache?

items.text: A scheduled break from the success feed
Screenshotting others' offers to brood over
Following people who share their struggles too

scenarios.relearn: Feed breaks and real celebration help; 2am scrolling and brooding fuel the ache.

scenarios.hook: Sort: noticing to learn from, or measuring your worth against them?

items.text: "How did she structure her prep? I'll borrow that"
"I can ask her what resources helped"
"Their approach is interesting; let me try it"
"Every win of theirs is a loss for me"

scenarios.relearn: Borrowing someone's method is learning; making their result a verdict on your worth is the trap.

scenarios.hook: Sort: what a success post actually shows, or what it hides?

items.text: The interview they bombed last week
The fear it won't work out

scenarios.relearn: A success post shows the offer, the caption and the photo; it hides the rejections, the bombed interview and the fear.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a steadying response to the comparison ache, or one that deepens it?

items.text: Naming the feeling: 'this is comparison, not truth'
Refreshing their profile to confirm you're behind
Returning to your own next small step
Replaying their win on a loop in your head
Texting a friend who feels it too
Deciding their success proves you've failed

scenarios.relearn: Naming the feeling steadies you; replaying their win deepens it.

scenarios.hook: Sort: what social media usually posts, or what it usually leaves out?

items.text: The backlog cleared on the third try
The therapy sessions and quiet panic
The year of feeling stuck before it

scenarios.relearn: Feeds post gowns, trips and promotions; they leave out the backlogs, the panic and the stuck years.

scenarios.hook: Sort: fits the comparison trap, or breaks out of it?

items.text: "My only race is with who I was yesterday"
"I'm a failure next to my batch"
"I can be glad for them and proud of me"
"There's a queue and I'm at the back"
"My behind-the-scenes is allowed to be messy"

scenarios.relearn: 'My race is with yesterday's me' and 'glad for them, proud of me' break out; 'failure next to my batch' stays trapped.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a thought that costs you nothing, or one that quietly costs your peace?

items.text: "Her offer is great news, full stop"
"His win means I'm running out of time"
"I can clap for them without keeping score"
"Every post is proof I'm not enough"
"Their good day isn't my bad day"
"I should already be where they are"

scenarios.relearn: Clapping for a win costs nothing; making every post proof you're behind costs your peace.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a real reason to feel behind, or just the comparison trap talking?

items.text: A goal you set yourself and missed
A stranger online living a different life
Feedback you actually got and can act on
A relative's idea of when you should 'settle'
A skill you genuinely want to build
A topper's reel the algorithm showed you

scenarios.relearn: Your goals and skills are real signals; strangers and topper reels are just the trap.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a fact about you, or a story the feed is selling you?

items.text: You showed up and did the work this week
You have people who care about you
"You're already too far behind to catch up"

scenarios.relearn: That you showed up, learned and are cared for are facts; 'everyone's sorted' and 'too far behind' are stories the feed sells.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy way to use someone's success, or the trap dressed as motivation?

items.text: Asking them which resources actually helped
Using their win to beat yourself up
Taking one idea from their approach to try
Refreshing their feed to feel worse on purpose
Letting their progress show a path is possible
Treating their result as your scorecard

scenarios.relearn: Asking what helped is healthy; using a win against yourself isn't.

scenarios.hook: Results are out. Half your group has posted offers, and you have none yet.

steps.prompt: Your phone lights up with another offer post. What do you do?

options.text: Scroll every post and count how far behind you are
options.then: You count twelve, and the knot tightens.

options.text: Reply to every group post with a cheerful message and hide your feelings
options.then: The replies keep coming, and you feel more alone.

options.text: Close the app, breathe, and message a friend in the same boat
options.then: She replies fast. "Me too. Can we talk?"

options.text: Ask a friend with an offer how she did it, right now
options.then: She's kind, but hearing her story at this moment stings.

steps.why: Stepping away and reaching someone in the same boat eases the spike.

steps.prompt: That evening, you want to do something about it. What do you do?

options.text: Apply to every open role you can find tonight
options.then: You send twelve forms, and can't tell which fits.

options.text: Wait until everyone's offers stop coming in
options.then: The offers keep coming, and so does the waiting.

options.text: Ask the group chat who got which salary and where
options.then: The numbers come in, and the gap looks bigger than before.

options.text: Write one or two things you can do this week
options.then: The list fits on a sticky note, and it feels doable.

steps.why: A short list gives your worry a shape you can work with.

steps.prompt: A week later, a friend from the group says she got an offer. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're fine and have no news to share
options.then: She nods, and you feel the gap between you grow.

options.text: Say you're about to get an offer of your own
options.then: She smiles, and you feel the small lie sit there.

options.text: Congratulate her and say you're still looking
options.then: She nods. "Thanks. I was nervous too, honestly."

options.text: Change the subject and leave soon
options.then: She watches you go, unsure what she said.

steps.why: Being happy for her and honest about yourself keeps the friendship steady.

steps.prompt: Another week on, the anxiety spikes at night. What do you do?

options.text: Scroll the placement groups to see if anything changed
options.then: New posts come in, and the spike gets worse.

options.text: Text a friend every worst case you can think of
options.then: Your friend replies kindly, but listing every fear made each one feel bigger.

options.text: Stay up planning every step for the next ten years
options.then: The plan fills a page, and it feels impossible by morning.

options.text: Breathe slowly, then write one next step
options.then: The step is small, and your shoulders drop a little.

steps.why: Breathing first and writing one step calms the spiral without pretending the worry isn't there.

scenarios.debrief: You're not the only one without news yet, and stepping back eases the spike.
scenarios.relearn: When the feed spikes you, step back and reach someone who gets it.

scenarios.hook: A close friend got into a programme you wanted, and you feel a real pang of envy.

steps.prompt: She shares the news in the group chat. What do you do?

options.text: Go quiet and let the envy cool things between you
options.then: The chat moves on, and she notices you haven't replied.

options.text: Reply with a thumbs-up and nothing else at all
options.then: She replies with a heart, and the distance stays.

options.text: Tell her it was probably easier for her to get in
options.then: She goes quiet, and the chat stops moving.

options.text: Send a real congratulations and keep the rest private
options.then: She replies with three hearts and a photo of the letter.

steps.why: A warm message protects the friendship, and your own feelings can wait for later.

steps.prompt: That night, the envy is still there. What do you do with it?

options.text: Tell yourself you shouldn't feel that at all
options.then: The feeling hides, and it comes back at 2 a.m.

options.text: Scroll her profile until it stops hurting
options.then: It doesn't stop, and you look at her photos for an hour.

options.text: Decide she only got in because of connections
options.then: The story feels fair, and it sours your view of her.

options.text: Name it, then write what you actually want
options.then: You write three lines, and two of them surprise you.

steps.why: Naming the envy shows you what you want, and that gives you a direction.

steps.prompt: She invites you to celebrate. What do you do?

options.text: Say you're busy this week and skip it
options.then: She sends a sad emoji, and the evening feels long.

options.text: Go, but sulk quietly through the whole dinner
options.then: She asks if you're all right, and you say "Fine."

options.text: Go and talk about your own rejection all evening
options.then: The night is about you, and she ends up quiet.

options.text: Go and ask her about the programme
options.then: She lights up, and the dinner feels warm.

steps.why: Being there for her, and asking about her news, keeps the friendship close.

scenarios.debrief: Their win isn't your loss, so be glad for them and hold your own feelings too.
scenarios.relearn: Celebrate a friend and feel your own pang. Both can be true at once.

scenarios.hook: Your feed is now mostly people whose lives make you feel small.

steps.prompt: It's Monday morning and the first post already stings. What do you do?

options.text: Brace yourself and keep scrolling to toughen up
options.then: By lunchtime, the sting has turned into a low mood.

options.text: Make a second account to keep watching them
options.then: You still see them all, and now have two feeds to check.

options.text: Unfollow only the ones you dislike and keep the ones who sting
options.then: The worst ones stay, and so does the sting.

options.text: Mute the accounts that sting and follow people who keep it real
options.then: The feed looks different, and the morning feels lighter.

steps.why: Choosing what you take in every day is a small, real kind of self-care.

steps.prompt: A friend says muting accounts is just hiding from reality. What do you say?

options.text: Agree, and never mute anyone so you stay tough
options.then: The sting stays, and the feed keeps shaping your mood.

options.text: Say he's right, and you're too sensitive
options.then: He laughs awkwardly, and you believe it a little.

options.text: Say choosing what you take in isn't hiding
options.then: He shrugs. "Fair. My feed could use that."

options.text: Say you'll quit social media completely
options.then: He looks doubtful, and you aren't sure either.

steps.why: You can see the world clearly without letting it shrink you each morning.

steps.prompt: That evening, you have an hour free. What do you do with it?

options.text: Wait for motivation to show up
options.then: The hour passes, and the motivation doesn't.

options.text: Fill the time with a huge new plan to catch up
options.then: The plan is big, and it feels heavy by the second day.

options.text: Pick one small thing you care about and do it
options.then: You spend an hour on it, and it feels like yours.

options.text: Check what your friends are doing instead
options.then: The hour goes to comparing, and it stings again.

steps.why: Doing one small thing you care about fills the space with something real.

scenarios.debrief: Your feed shapes your mood, and curating it away from shame-triggers is self-care.
scenarios.relearn: Curate your feed toward what steadies you, not what shames you.

scenarios.hook: A relative lists every "settled" cousin and asks why you aren't there yet.

steps.prompt: She finishes the list and waits for your answer. What do you do?

options.text: Take it as proof you've fallen behind and spiral after
options.then: The list plays in your head all evening.

options.text: List your own achievements to match the cousins
options.then: She nods politely, and the talk turns into a contest.

options.text: Say warmly that you're on a different path at your own pace
options.then: She blinks. "Hm. Well, everyone is different."

options.text: Laugh it off and change the subject
options.then: She lets it go, and the question waits for next time.

steps.why: A warm, steady answer holds your path without starting a fight.

steps.prompt: After she leaves, your mother asks what you think. What do you say?

options.text: Say nothing, since it's not worth a conversation
options.then: She studies your face, and the ache stays with you.

options.text: Agree that you should be further ahead by now
options.then: She says "No, no," but the room feels heavy.

options.text: Say Aunty is a gossip and you won't see her again
options.then: Your mother sighs, and the evening turns tense.

options.text: Say it stung, and you'd like to share your plans
options.then: She sits down. "Tell me. I'd like to hear them."

steps.why: Saying it stung and sharing your plans lets your mother stand with you.

steps.prompt: That night, the cousins' photos fill the family group. What do you do?

options.text: Scroll every post and measure yourself against them
options.then: The hour leaves you tired and low.

options.text: Post your own news to match theirs
options.then: The likes come in, and the feeling doesn't change.

options.text: Put the phone away and do one thing on your own list
options.then: You finish one small task, and it feels like yours.

options.text: Message Aunty to explain your plans in detail
options.then: She replies with a thumbs-up, and you feel unheard.

steps.why: Doing one thing for your own list keeps you focused on your pace, not theirs.

steps.prompt: A month later, Aunty asks again at another function. What do you do?

options.text: Dodge her for the entire function by staying busy
options.then: You spend the evening in the kitchen, and she notices.

options.text: Give her a detailed plan to settle the question
options.then: She has more questions, and the talk goes on for half an hour.

options.text: Argue that she's wrong to compare people at all
options.then: The room goes quiet, and she says she only meant well.

options.text: Smile, say you're doing well, and ask about her
options.then: She tells you about her garden, and the question doesn't come back.

steps.why: A warm answer, plus a question about her, turns the talk to something kinder.

scenarios.debrief: A relative's timeline isn't yours, so hold your own path gently.
scenarios.relearn: Hold your pace warmly. A relative's timeline isn't a verdict on yours.

scenarios.hook: It's late, and you've spent an hour comparing your year to everyone's reels.

steps.prompt: It's past midnight and your eyes hurt. What do you do?

options.text: Keep scrolling to confirm just how behind you are
options.then: The scroll goes on, and so does the hollow feeling.

options.text: Set a timer for ten more minutes of reels
options.then: The timer goes off, and you set it again.

options.text: Put the phone down and write one thing you did
options.then: You write "finished the course," and it feels solid.

options.text: Start a big "new me" plan in your notes app
options.then: The plan is long, and it feels impossible by morning.

steps.why: Naming one real thing reconnects you with your actual year, not an edited one.

steps.prompt: The next morning, the feeling is still there. What do you do?

options.text: Check the reels again to see if you were wrong
options.then: The reels look the same, and the feeling returns.

options.text: Promise yourself you'll fix everything starting tomorrow
options.then: The promise sits there, and tomorrow looks heavy.

options.text: Skip breakfast and work all day to catch up
options.then: By evening, you're exhausted and snappy.

options.text: Take a short walk, then do one small thing
options.then: The walk clears your head, and the small task takes twenty minutes.

steps.why: A short walk and one small task give you a real start.

steps.prompt: That evening, a friend says she's been feeling behind too. What do you do?

options.text: Say she isn't behind, and you are the one who is
options.then: She looks puzzled, and the conversation tilts toward you.

options.text: Say everyone feels this, so there's no need to talk
options.then: She nods, and the talk ends early.

options.text: Send her reels that made you feel better about it
options.then: She watches them, and the reels are still in both of your phones.

options.text: Share your night, and plan a screen-free hour
options.then: She laughs. "Yes. Tomorrow, at six."

steps.why: Sharing it, and planning a screen-free hour together, takes the pressure off both of you.

scenarios.debrief: Reels are edits, and refocusing on your own real progress steadies you.
scenarios.relearn: When reels leave you hollow, name one real thing you did.

scenarios.hook: You're about to text a friend that everyone's ahead and you're panicking.

steps.prompt: Your thumb hovers over Send. What do you do?

options.text: Delete it and carry the weight quietly
