scenarios.hook: Placement results are out, and Sunday's family lunch feels like a scoreboard.

steps.prompt: Over lunch an uncle says your cousin's package is far bigger than yours. What do you do?

options.text: Stay steady: different paths, and I'm okay with mine
options.then: The table moves on. The comparison loses its grip.

options.text: Decide he's right and that you're worth less
options.then: The food goes down in silence, and your shoulders slump.

options.text: Quote your own salary back at him, defensively
options.then: You win a moment, and the lunch turns tense.

options.text: Leave the table quietly without saying anything
options.then: You hide in the kitchen. Your mother notices and follows.

steps.why: A package is a status marker, not a verdict on your worth.

steps.prompt: Later, your cousin messages to ask if the lunch bothered you. What do you do?

options.text: Say it stung, and that you're okay with your path
options.then: He replies, "Sorry. I didn't choose that comparison either."

options.text: Say it didn't bother you at all, honestly
options.then: He believes you. The sting stays unspoken.

options.text: Ask how much he earns, to compare properly
options.then: He tells you. You feel smaller, and it doesn't help.

options.text: Ignore the message entirely and leave it unread
options.then: He wonders what he did. The distance grows.

steps.why: Saying the real feeling lets you keep the friendship.

steps.prompt: Your mother says relatives mean well and you should earn more. What do you do?

options.text: Say you hear her worry, and say what matters to you
options.then: She listens, thoughtful. "I only want you to be secure."

options.text: Promise to earn more soon, so she can relax
options.then: She relaxes. You carry a promise you can't control.

options.text: Stay quiet and let it pass without saying anything
options.then: She reads your silence as agreement.

options.text: Tell her the relatives are all rather shallow people
options.then: She stiffens. "They're family. Don't say that."

steps.why: Your worth is separate from your package, and you can say so kindly.

scenarios.debrief: A package is a status marker, not a verdict on your worth.
scenarios.relearn: Your worth isn't graded by how your package compares.

scenarios.hook: Placement day is here, and you've pinned a lot on the first round.

steps.prompt: The list is out and your name isn't on it. What do you do?

options.text: Name the feeling, and remember you're more than a placement
options.then: The sting stays. It stops being the only thing about you.

options.text: Conclude that this result means you're worthless now
options.then: The thought repeats, louder, through the evening.

options.text: Hide in your room and skip every single message
options.then: The room is quiet, and so are your friends' worried texts.

options.text: Send an angry message to the recruiter tonight
options.then: The message goes out. It changes nothing, and adds embarrassment.

steps.why: One placement round is an outcome, not a verdict on your worth.

steps.prompt: Batchmates are celebrating in the corridor. What do you do?

options.text: Congratulate them, then step away for air
options.then: Their joy is real, and so is your need for air.

options.text: Fake a smile and stay through all of the party
options.then: The smile holds until the stairwell, where it cracks.

options.text: Avoid them for days and skip the corridor too
options.then: The days drag, and the distance feels heavier than the list.

options.text: Tell them that the process was unfair all along
options.then: They nod awkwardly. The party loses a little of its glow.

steps.why: You can be glad for others and still need space.

steps.prompt: A senior suggests you look at feedback and plan the next round. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what you can learn, and plan one next step
options.then: He gives you two pointers. You keep one.

options.text: Say there's no point in trying again
options.then: He shrugs sadly. The door shuts from your side.

options.text: Ask him to tell you what's wrong with you
options.then: He says that is not how it works. You feel worse.

options.text: Send forty applications overnight
options.then: The pile looks busy. Most of them are scattershot.

steps.why: Treat a setback as information, then take one small step.

steps.prompt: That night a heavy "I'm nobody now" feeling sets in. What do you do?

options.text: Talk to someone you trust. Tele-MANAS 14416 helps
options.then: You message a friend. The feeling is smaller when it's shared.

options.text: Stay up replaying the whole day over and over
options.then: By 3am the replay is louder than the day was.

options.text: Decide this proves you'll never get anywhere
options.then: You close every tab. The thought sits heavier, and you feel more alone.

options.text: Scroll the placed list again and again and again
options.then: Each scroll is another small wound.

steps.why: When it gets heavy, reaching out is smart. It isn't your fault, and your worth was never a rank.

steps.prompt: Months later a new round opens. What do you do?

options.text: Try again, here or elsewhere, with one change
options.then: You adjust one line of the plan and move. It's a step, not a verdict.

options.text: Skip it, as proof you were never good enough
options.then: You let it pass. The hurt calls it proof, but it's a feeling, not a fact.

options.text: Apply to beat your batchmates
options.then: Every reply becomes a scoreboard. The pressure builds.

options.text: Send the same application as before
options.then: Nothing changes, and you wonder why.

steps.why: Move on with one adjustment, wherever it leads. A setback is a comma, not a full stop.

scenarios.debrief: A placement round is one outcome, not a measure of your worth.
scenarios.relearn: Not getting placed in a round doesn't make you 'nobody'.

scenarios.hook: Placement season is ending, and your phone buzzes twice in one afternoon.

steps.prompt: Two offers arrive: one with a famous title, and a smaller role you'd enjoy. What do you do?

options.text: Weigh fit and values, not only what impresses
options.then: You list what matters to you. The list looks nothing like the job titles.

options.text: Take the title purely for the status it carries
options.then: You lean towards it at once, though a flicker of unease stays with you.

options.text: Ask your loudest relative to decide for you
options.then: She picks the title in seconds. You wonder what you'd have chosen.

options.text: Flip a coin so you don't have to decide
options.then: The coin lands. You spend the evening arguing with it.

steps.why: Fit matters more than status when a title is all that's pulling you.

steps.prompt: Before you reply to either offer, a friend says the smaller role will look weak on a CV. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what she means, then check it against your goals
options.then: She explains, and you weigh it honestly against what you want.

options.text: Agree, and take the title to look stronger
options.then: You nod. The worry about how it looks outweighs your own reasons.

options.text: Dismiss her and stop asking anyone
options.then: You miss the useful part of her advice.

options.text: Ask five more friends until one agrees with you
options.then: The fifth agrees. You learn nothing new.

steps.why: Listen to advice, then test it against what you actually value.

steps.prompt: A month in, your choice feels uncertain on a hard day. What do you do?

options.text: Review what you chose it for, and adjust
options.then: You look at why you picked it. Some of it still holds, and you change one small thing.

options.text: Treat the doubt as proof that you chose wrong
options.then: One hard day begins to look like a verdict.

options.text: Hide the doubt and push through it, quietly
options.then: You push through. The doubt waits and grows.

options.text: Compare your choice with everyone else's
options.then: Their choices look cleaner than yours. They always do.

steps.why: Doubt on a hard day is normal information, not a verdict.

scenarios.debrief: Fit matters more than status when a title is the only thing pulling you.
scenarios.relearn: Choose for fit and values, not a title that only impresses others.

scenarios.hook: Your whole mood is swinging with each test score this term.

steps.prompt: A result is due tomorrow and you can't sleep. What do you do?

options.text: Anchor your worth in who you are, apart from the score
options.then: You still care about tomorrow. You stop staking yourself on it.

options.text: Keep letting the score decide how much you're worth
options.then: You hold your breath all night, waiting for a number.

options.text: Refresh the marks portal every hour
options.then: Each refresh is another small jolt of dread.

options.text: Promise yourself a treat only for a high score
options.then: The treat hangs over you, and so does its absence.

steps.why: Steady worth doesn't rise with a good score or fall with a bad one.

steps.prompt: The score is lower than you hoped. What do you do?

options.text: Feel the disappointment, then check what to adjust
options.then: The disappointment passes. One idea is left to try.

options.text: Decide you're not cut out for any of this
options.then: The thought gets louder each time you open a book.

options.text: Hide it and avoid your friends for a while
options.then: The hiding is tiring and lonely.

options.text: Blame the teacher and the paper for the score
options.then: It feels better briefly. The next test still comes.

steps.why: A score is information about one test, not about you.

steps.prompt: Next week a friend gets top marks and you feel small. What do you do?

options.text: Congratulate her, and do something you value
options.then: Her smile is real. So is your own evening.

options.text: Pretend that you don't care about it at all
options.then: The pretending is tiring, and it shows.

options.text: Count exactly how many points you trail her by
options.then: The number becomes the only thing you see.

options.text: Stop studying with her, and study alone now
options.then: You study alone, and she wonders why.

steps.why: Celebrating others costs you nothing, and your worth is not a score.

scenarios.debrief: Steady worth doesn't rise with a good score or fall with a bad one.
scenarios.relearn: Anchor your worth in who you are, not in each test score.

scenarios.hook: Your close friend Nikhil has just got his dream offer, and you feel suddenly small beside him.

steps.prompt: He shows you the offer letter, beaming. What do you do?

options.text: Congratulate him, then let the sting settle
options.then: Nikhil hugs you. Later, the sting has faded a little.

options.text: Congratulate him, then apply to ten places tonight
options.then: You send ten rushed applications at midnight and feel more anxious.

options.text: Smile fast and change the subject
options.then: Nikhil goes quiet for a second. You leave early, still feeling small.

options.text: Ask how many others he beat for it
options.then: He shrugs, a little hurt. The offer starts to feel like a scoreboard.

steps.why: Your worth doesn't shrink beside his win. Feel the sting, then steady yourself.

steps.prompt: Days later, your batch group is full of offer screenshots. What do you do?

options.text: Leave the group so you never see offers again
options.then: It's quiet, but you miss the jokes and feel cut off from friends.

options.text: Scroll through every offer to see where you stand
options.then: An hour passes. You feel further behind and have done nothing.

options.text: Reply with cheers and keep scrolling all night
options.then: You cheer for everyone and sleep badly, still checking the chat.

options.text: Mute it for today and take one step of your own
options.then: The chat goes quiet. You finish a small task and feel steadier.

steps.why: Stepping back from the highlight reel gives your own path room to move.

steps.prompt: Nikhil invites you to a small celebration dinner on Saturday. What do you do?

options.text: Go, but leave early before anyone asks your plans
options.then: You dodge the question, and the night feels like a test you slipped out of.

options.text: Go and talk up a half-made plan to look equal
options.then: You oversell your plan. Driving home, you feel like you're performing.

options.text: Go, celebrate him, and say you've felt behind too
options.then: He laughs softly. "Me too, honestly. I was terrified before this."

options.text: Skip it, since you can't fake being happy
options.then: Nikhil texts "Next time?" You spend Saturday alone with the feeling.

steps.why: Celebrating him costs nothing, and honesty with a friend eases the sting.

scenarios.debrief: Someone else's win is not a measure of your value.
scenarios.relearn: A friend's offer doesn't make you 'less than'; your worth is yours.

scenarios.hook: You love painting, but a senior says it won't look good on a CV.

steps.prompt: The art club sign-up closes today. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it this year and promise to paint later
options.then: The deadline passes. Your sketchbook stays shut on the shelf.

options.text: Join a CV-friendly club instead
options.then: The new club looks good on paper. Your brushes stay in the drawer.

options.text: Ask three seniors which club looks best
options.then: Each says something different. The deadline nears and you feel more muddled.

options.text: Join, because it's part of who you are
options.then: You sign up. The first evening in the studio feels like a long breath out.

steps.why: What you love is part of you, and it doesn't need a CV line to count.

steps.prompt: A friend sees your sketchbook and says to share it online. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's just a hobby and not worth posting
options.then: Your friend shrugs. You close the sketchbook, feeling oddly flat.

options.text: Wait until it's good enough to call a portfolio
options.then: The bar keeps moving. Weeks pass with no new pages.

options.text: Share one piece, just because you like it
options.then: A few friends comment warmly. You feel a little lighter.

options.text: Share only after checking it would impress recruiters
options.then: You delete three pieces you loved. What's left feels like it isn't yours.

steps.why: Sharing something because you like it keeps it yours, not a line for recruiters.

steps.prompt: Placement season starts, and everyone is trimming their lives down to CV lines. What do you do?

options.text: Keep painting in secret and never mention it
options.then: You paint late at night, half guilty, as if it were something to hide.

options.text: Keep painting and mention it only if it fits
options.then: You paint on Sundays. It steadies you through the stressful weeks.

options.text: Stop painting until placements are over
options.then: The weeks go by. The pull stays, and the canvas stays blank.

options.text: Turn it into a side business so it counts
options.then: Orders stack up and the joy thins. Painting starts to feel like work.

steps.why: You can keep what you love without turning it into a product.

scenarios.debrief: Your life isn't only the parts that fit a CV.
scenarios.relearn: You're allowed to value parts of yourself that never reach a CV.

scenarios.hook: You catch yourself introducing friends only by their college and package.

steps.prompt: At a family gathering, your cousin asks who your new friends are. What do you say?

options.text: Mention only the ones with big offers
options.then: Your cousin looks impressed. You realise you left out your closest friend.

options.text: Scold yourself for the habit and say nothing
options.then: You freeze, and the talk moves on. You feel worse about the habit.

options.text: Name them and say what you enjoy about each
options.then: Your cousin smiles. "Sounds like good company." You feel warmer.

options.text: Give their colleges and expected packages first
options.then: Your cousin nods and compares. Your friends start to sound like ranks.

steps.why: Seeing people as people loosens the scoreboard you use on yourself.

steps.prompt: At a hostel get-together, a friend from a smaller college is called "not placed yet". What do you do?

options.text: Message him later that it was rude, saying nothing there
options.then: He replies "Thanks." In the room itself, nothing had changed for him.

options.text: Turn to him and ask what he's been into lately
options.then: His face brightens. He tells you about a project he's been building.

options.text: Laugh along so the mood stays light
options.then: He laughs too, stiffly. He picks up his phone and goes quiet.

options.text: Loudly say he's more than that and walk out
options.then: The room freezes. Nobody asks him a thing after you leave.

steps.why: Asking about the person, not the label, shows them they're seen.

steps.prompt: You notice you still rank yourself in your head whenever someone shares news. What do you try?

options.text: Name one thing about them that isn't a number
options.then: You note a friend's humour. The news feels less like a contest.

options.text: Promise yourself you'll never compare again
options.then: By evening you've broken it, and you feel worse for it.

options.text: Avoid people's news for a while
options.then: Fewer updates help a little, but you feel cut off from friends.

options.text: Rank yourself kindly and give yourself a top spot
options.then: It feels good for a minute. The scoreboard is still running in your head.

steps.why: Noticing the habit and naming a non-number quality turns ranking into seeing.

scenarios.debrief: When you stop ranking others by CV, you stop grading yourself.
scenarios.relearn: People, you included, are more than their college and package.

scenarios.hook: At a family function, Mausi says she'll be proud once you're settled in a big job.

steps.prompt: Everyone nearby smiles and waits for your reply. What do you say?

options.text: Change the subject to the food
options.then: Everyone laughs and moves on. The comment stays with you all evening.

options.text: Thank her and say you matter as you are
options.then: Mausi blinks, then chuckles. "Arre, of course you do." Others nod.

options.text: Say "I'll make you proud. Just wait."
options.then: She beams. The words sit in your chest like a debt.

options.text: Argue that her pride sounds shallow
options.then: The table goes silent. Your mother gives you a hard look.

steps.why: Your worth holds now. You can say so gently without a fight.

steps.prompt: That night your mother says, "Mausi only wants the best for you." What do you do?

options.text: Say you know it's care, and explain how it lands
options.then: She pauses. "I didn't think it sounded like that to you."

options.text: Nod and say you'll work harder
options.then: She relaxes. You lie awake feeling the bar go up.

options.text: Say Mausi is old-fashioned and end the talk
options.then: Your mother sighs. The matter is closed and so is the conversation.

options.text: Say you're fine and keep the sting to yourself
options.then: She goes to bed content. The sting stays unspoken.

steps.why: Acknowledging the care while sharing how it lands keeps you close and honest.

steps.prompt: Months later, you have a rough exam week and Mausi's line returns. What do you do?

options.text: Decide you'll matter once the job arrives
options.then: The week feels like a waiting room. Your chest stays tight.

options.text: Push harder and cut sleep to fix the result
options.then: You stay up late, and focus slips further with the tiredness.

options.text: Keep it to yourself until the results are out
options.then: You carry it alone for days. The results don't lift the heaviness.

options.text: Tell yourself it's not true and call a friend
options.then: Your friend says you're not your marks. The knot loosens a little.

steps.why: When a bad week hits, a steadying truth and a friend help more than waiting it out alone.

scenarios.debrief: Worth conditional on a job is fragile; yours holds steady regardless.
scenarios.relearn: Your worth holds now, not only once you're 'settled'.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a mark sheet can grade one test. It was never built to grade you.
scenarios.prompt: Sit with that for a second.
scenarios.affirm: You are a whole person a mark sheet was never designed to measure.
scenarios.relearn: A mark sheet grades a test, not the person who sat it.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: name one thing about you that no CV could ever capture.
scenarios.affirm: That part of you is real worth, and no resume has a column for it.
scenarios.relearn: Your realest worth is the part no CV has a column for.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: think of someone you love. Do you love their rank, or them?
scenarios.affirm: You love people for who they are, and that's exactly how worth works for you too.
scenarios.relearn: You love people for who they are, not their rank; the same is true of your worth.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: your worth was here before your first exam and stays after your last.
scenarios.affirm: Your worth doesn't start at an admit card or end at a result; it's just yours.
scenarios.relearn: Your worth exists before and after any exam, independent of results.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: if a friend got your exact result, would you call them worthless?
scenarios.affirm: The kindness you'd give a friend is the kindness your own worth deserves too.
scenarios.relearn: You wouldn't call a friend worthless for a result; offer yourself that same truth.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: picture your worth as a floor, not an elevator that moves with scores.
scenarios.affirm: Your worth is a steady floor, not an elevator riding up and down with results.
scenarios.relearn: Worth is a steady floor, not an elevator that moves with each score.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: in ten years, which will you remember, your CGPA or who stood by you?
scenarios.affirm: The things that hold your worth are the ones that outlast any number on a transcript.
scenarios.relearn: What holds your worth outlasts any number on a transcript.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Riya has just seen a low semester result.
scenarios.setup: She sits down beside you, her eyes red.

steps.prompt: Riya says: "I'm a failure. Everyone else passed easily."

options.text: "It's nothing. Don't cry over marks, yaar."
options.then: She wipes her eyes. "It's not nothing to me."

options.text: "Let's fix your study plan right now."
options.then: She sighs. "I can't think about plans. I just feel awful."

options.text: "A bad semester isn't a verdict on you. I'm here."
options.then: She sniffs. "It really feels like it is, though."

options.text: "Yeah, that's rough. Low results don't look great."
options.then: She nods slowly. "So I am behind. I knew it."

steps.why: A result isn't a verdict, and hearing that from a friend matters most.

steps.prompt: Riya says: "My parents will be so disappointed in me."

options.text: "They'll understand. Don't worry about it at all."
options.then: She manages a small nod. "You don't know that."

options.text: "That sounds heavy. Want to plan the talk together?"
options.then: She breathes out. "Yes. I keep imagining the worst."

options.text: "Hide it until you've got a fix sorted out."
options.then: She chews her lip. "They'll find out anyway, right?"

options.text: "They'll be furious. Brace yourself for it."
options.then: Her face falls. "I was trying not to think about that."

steps.why: Offering to plan the conversation together supports her without hiding or scaring her.

steps.prompt: Riya says: "I keep thinking this is the end for me."

options.text: "That's so heavy. Can we see the counsellor?"
options.then: She nods, eyes wet. "Okay. I'd rather not go alone."

options.text: "Everyone feels like that. Just push through it."
options.then: She nods stiffly. "Right." She goes quiet and doesn't say much else that evening.

options.text: "Don't be dramatic. Sleep on it."
options.then: She pulls back. "Forget I said anything."

options.text: "Let's watch a film and forget it tonight, okay?"
options.then: She laughs a little. Halfway through, she's staring at the wall again.

steps.why: When it feels that heavy, a counsellor or Tele-MANAS 14416 is real support, and it's never her fault.

scenarios.relearn: Help a friend separate a result from who they are.

scenarios.hook: Your uncle Mahesh keeps asking about your package before anything else.
scenarios.setup: At the wedding lunch, he beckons you over.

steps.prompt: Uncle Mahesh asks: "What package will you get? That's what matters."

options.text: "Ask me after placements, Uncle."
options.then: He waves a hand. "I will. Don't forget to tell me."

options.text: "My worth isn't just a salary number, Uncle."
options.then: He blinks. "Hmm. I didn't mean it that way."

options.text: "A big one, I hope. Then you'll be proud."
options.then: He claps your shoulder. The number now feels like your price tag.

options.text: "Why is money all you people talk about?"
options.then: His face hardens. "Careful, beta. I'm older than you."

steps.why: Gently naming your worth gives him a chance to see more than a number.

steps.prompt: Your cousin whispers: "Just give him a number. It stops the questions."

options.text: "I'd like him to know me beyond the number too."
options.then: Your cousin shrugs. "Good luck with that." But she smiles.

options.text: "Fine, I'll give a number to keep the peace."
options.then: She nods. The questions stop, and the number feels like a mask.

options.text: "I'll make up a big number to impress him."
options.then: She raises her eyebrows. "Then you'll have to live up to it."

options.text: "Let's avoid him for the rest of lunch."
options.then: You slip away. He finds you by the dessert table anyway.

steps.why: You don't have to shrink to a number, and you don't have to hide from him either.

steps.prompt: Later, Uncle Mahesh catches you by the sweets. "Beta, what do you actually enjoy?"

options.text: "Nothing much. A good package, like you said."
options.then: He nods, satisfied. You feel oddly empty.

options.text: "Honestly, nothing you'd approve of."
options.then: He stiffens. "Who said I wouldn't approve?"

options.text: "I'm not sure, Uncle. Let's not get into it."
options.then: He shrugs. "As you like." The chance slips by.

options.text: "I enjoy building things. Can I show you?"
options.then: He looks surprised, then pleased. "Tell me more."

steps.why: Sharing one real thing lets him see you, not just your package.

scenarios.relearn: Keep your worth steady even when others tie pride to your package.

scenarios.hook: Your junior Tanvi didn't crack the exam she prepared for over two years.
scenarios.setup: She finds you in the library corridor.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says: "I'm nothing now. I didn't crack it."

options.text: "One exam can't decide who you are."
options.then: She looks up. "It felt like it decided everything."

options.text: "Honestly, that exam probably shows where you stand."
options.then: She looks away. "Then I really am nothing."

options.text: "Don't say that. Lots of people don't crack it."
options.then: She nods faintly. "Lots of people aren't me, though."

options.text: "Let's look at other exams you can give."
options.then: She winces. "I can't think about the next one yet."

steps.why: One exam can't decide who she is, and she needs that said plainly.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says: "My family spent so much on coaching for me."

options.text: "Then make it worth it with a stronger attempt."
options.then: She swallows. "Stronger. Right." She looks more tired.

options.text: "They'll get over it. Don't feel guilty."
options.then: She shrugs. "I still do."

options.text: "Then tell them right now that you'll retry."
options.then: She stiffens. "Right now? I haven't even thought."

options.text: "That's heavy to carry. Your worth isn't their fee."
options.then: Her eyes fill. "I needed someone to say that."

steps.why: Her worth isn't what was spent, and naming that lifts some of the weight.

steps.prompt: Tanvi asks: "What do I even do now?"

options.text: "Nothing. Just wait and see what happens."
options.then: She shrugs. "Okay." Days pass and the heaviness stays.

options.text: "Retry the same exam right away, no break."
options.then: She looks dizzy. "Maybe. I don't know. I'm so tired."

options.text: "Rest first. Then one small step, with a mentor."
options.then: She breathes out. "One small step. I can try that."

options.text: "Plan your whole next year tonight."
options.then: She looks overwhelmed. "That's too much tonight."

steps.why: Rest first, then one small step with guidance, is steadier than a rushed plan.

scenarios.relearn: Remind someone an exam can't decide who they are.

scenarios.hook: Your neighbour Vikas bhaiya likes to rank everyone in the building by salary.
scenarios.setup: He stops you on the stairs, smiling.

steps.prompt: Vikas bhaiya says: "Get a big package first. Then I'll respect you."

options.text: "Okay then. I'll show you very soon."
options.then: He grins. "That's the spirit." The clock in your head starts.

options.text: "Who needs your respect anyway?"
options.then: His smile vanishes. "Wah. Such attitude."

options.text: "Thanks, bhaiya. I'll keep that in mind."
options.then: He nods, pleased. You climb the stairs feeling smaller.

options.text: "My worth isn't earned with a package, bhaiya."
options.then: He laughs, surprised. "Arre, I was joking. Mostly."

steps.why: Your worth isn't something a package earns, and you can say so calmly.

steps.prompt: Later your friend asks: "Did that bother you?"

options.text: "Yes. Maybe he's right about me."
options.then: She winces. "He's not. But you're going to think so."

options.text: "Yes. Now I have to prove him wrong."
options.then: She sighs. "That's his scoreboard, though."

options.text: "A bit, but my worth isn't his view."
options.then: She smiles. "Good. He says it to everyone."

options.text: "Not at all. I felt nothing."
options.then: She tilts her head. "Really? Your face said otherwise."

steps.why: Being honest about the sting, and holding your worth steady, is the healthy reply.

steps.prompt: Next week Vikas bhaiya says: "Package yet? I'm only motivating you, you know."

options.text: "Okay, bhaiya. No problem. Let's move on."
options.then: He claps your arm and leaves. Nothing has changed.

options.text: "I know. Encourage me without the price tag?"
options.then: He scratches his head. "Hmm. Fair. I can try that."

options.text: "You're right. I need the push."
options.then: He nods. You swallow the last of what you wanted to say.

options.text: "Stop. Don't talk to me again."
options.then: His eyebrows shoot up. "What did I say?"

steps.why: You can ask for kind encouragement without a price tag.

scenarios.relearn: Your worth doesn't wait on a package to become real.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Mira keeps shrinking herself beside her topper roommate, Anika.
scenarios.setup: After Anika's award, Mira sits quietly beside you.

steps.prompt: Mira says: "Anika won again. Next to her, I'm nothing."

options.text: "Stop comparing yourself. It's honestly silly."
options.then: Mira goes quiet. "Silly? It doesn't feel silly."

options.text: "Then go and win something yourself, Mira."
options.then: She laughs bitterly. "What, by next week?"

options.text: "Her win doesn't shrink you. It's not a race."
options.then: Mira sniffs. "It feels like a race, though."

options.text: "Yeah, next to her you do look a bit behind."
options.then: Mira's face falls. "I knew it. Everyone sees it."

steps.why: Her win doesn't shrink Mira, and hearing that reframes the comparison.

steps.prompt: Mira says: "At the party, everyone asked only about Anika."

options.text: "Skip parties like that from now on."
options.then: She nods. "Maybe." She looks lonelier at the thought.

options.text: "That stung. You're more than who they ask about."
options.then: She nods slowly. "I needed to hear that."

options.text: "Ignore them. They're all fake."
options.then: She shrugs. "They're not. They're just people."

options.text: "Then try to be a bit more like Anika, maybe."
options.then: Her shoulders drop. "I've tried. It doesn't fit me."

steps.why: Naming the sting and what she is beyond it gives her ground to stand on.

steps.prompt: Mira asks: "Should I even stay friends with Anika?"

options.text: "Yes. Her win is hers. Yours will be yours."
options.then: Mira smiles slightly. "I'll try seeing her wins as hers."

options.text: "No. Keep your distance from toppers."
options.then: She sighs. "But she's kind to me. That's the odd part."

options.text: "Yes, but only to copy her study methods."
options.then: She frowns. "Copying feels like losing again."

options.text: "Ask her to stop mentioning her wins."
options.then: She pauses. "That's unfair to Anika, isn't it?"

steps.why: The comparing is the problem, not Anika, so Mira can keep the friend and loosen the contest.

scenarios.relearn: Someone's worth isn't a competition with a high-achiever.

scenarios.hook: A rejection email lands in your inbox, and your harshest inner voice starts up.
scenarios.setup: You're alone at your desk, reading it once more.

steps.prompt: Your inner critic says: "They rejected you. Face it. You're not good enough."

options.text: "It's fine. Totally fine. Moving on right now."
options.then: The voice murmurs. "Sure. Then why are your hands shaking?"

options.text: "That stung. It's information, not a verdict."
options.then: The voice quiets. "Okay. It did sting."

options.text: "You're right. I'm clearly not good enough."
options.then: The voice sharpens. "See? I told you."

options.text: "Stop. I refuse to feel anything about this."
options.then: The voice hisses. "You can't shut me up that easily."

steps.why: A rejection is information, and you can say so to yourself like a kind friend would.

steps.prompt: Your inner critic says: "Everyone else got in. What's wrong with you?"

options.text: "Nothing's wrong. People post wins, not doubts."
options.then: The voice pauses. "That's... true, actually."

options.text: "Everything, probably. I should quit applying."
options.then: The voice softens into a sigh. "Then why did you try at all?"

options.text: "I'll find the flaw and fix it tonight."
options.then: The voice perks up. "Good. Stay up. Dig through everything."

options.text: "Nothing. I'm just unlucky. That's all."
options.then: The voice scoffs. "Luck again. Sure."

steps.why: You see others' wins, not their doubts, and a rejection isn't a verdict on you.

steps.prompt: By morning, your inner critic says: "So what now? Are you quitting?"

options.text: "Yes. I'm done with applications for good."
options.then: The voice goes flat. "Fine." The quiet that follows feels heavy, not peaceful.

options.text: "Apply to twenty more right now."
options.then: The voice cackles. "Sure. Burn out by midnight."

options.text: "Wait and see if motivation turns up."
options.then: The voice yawns. "Then we wait a long time."

options.text: "Rest today. Tomorrow, one small next step."
options.then: The voice goes quiet. "One step. Fine. That sounds doable."

steps.why: Rest and one small next step beat both quitting and a panicked rush.

scenarios.relearn: Talk to yourself after a rejection the way a kind friend would.

scenarios.hook: At a family function, your uncle introduces you to guests only by your marks and college.
scenarios.setup: A guest turns to you with a polite smile.

steps.prompt: Your uncle tells a guest: "Top marks, good college. That says it all."

options.text: "There's more to me than marks. I'd like to be known too."
options.then: The guest smiles. "Oh, I'd like that. Tell me."

options.text: "Yes, that's all there is to me."
options.then: The guest nods, already turning away. You feel smaller.

options.text: "Uncle, please stop introducing me like that."
options.then: Your uncle frowns. "What did I say wrong?" The guest looks awkward.

options.text: "I'll tell you more once I've got a job."
options.then: The guest nods politely. "Of course. Do let us know."

steps.why: You can add the part of you that isn't a stat, politely and in the moment.

steps.prompt: At the buffet, the guest finds you again and asks: "So what do you enjoy, outside studies?"

options.text: "Nothing. Just studying, really."
options.then: The guest says "Hm, good." The conversation fades.

options.text: "Oh, it's not worth mentioning."
options.then: The guest shrugs kindly and drifts off toward the desserts.

options.text: "Only things that look good on a CV."
options.then: "Such as?" You list three, and none of them is yours.

options.text: "I fix old phones for friends. I love it."
options.then: "Really?" The guest leans in. "My phone has been dead for months."

steps.why: Sharing a real interest lets people meet you, not just your record.

steps.prompt: Later your uncle says: "I only wanted them to know you're doing well."

options.text: "Then you don't really know me at all."
options.then: His face closes. "That's not fair, beta."

options.text: "It's fine. Next time, just say less."
options.then: He shrugs. "As you like." He doesn't ask what you meant.

options.text: "I know. I'd like them to know me as a person too."
options.then: He pauses. "I suppose I never asked what you like."

options.text: "Sorry, Uncle. I'll stick to marks next time."
options.then: He nods, pleased. You feel the box close around you.

steps.why: Telling him kindly that you want to be known as a person helps him see you more fully.

scenarios.relearn: You're more than the marks and college others introduce you by.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Sahil has been low since the mock test ranks came out.
scenarios.setup: You walk back from coaching class together.

steps.prompt: Sahil says: "If I had a better rank, I'd be a better person."

options.text: "True. A better rank probably would make you better."
options.then: He nods, then sighs. "So I'm not good enough yet."

options.text: "Stop being so dramatic about a number."
options.then: He pulls back. "It's not just a number to me."

options.text: "Then work harder and you'll be that person."
options.then: He smiles thinly. "I'm already working every hour."

options.text: "A rank can't make you better. You already are good."
options.then: He looks at you. "You really think so?"

steps.why: Rank and character are different things, and he needs that said plainly.

steps.prompt: Sahil says: "My parents treat me better when my scores are up."

options.text: "Your parents are unfair. Ignore them."
options.then: He shakes his head. "I can't ignore my own parents."

options.text: "They're just worried. It's not personal."
options.then: He shrugs. "It feels personal when it's my own parents."

options.text: "That hurts. You're the same either way."
options.then: His voice cracks. "I wish they saw it that way."

options.text: "Then just keep your scores up."
options.then: He laughs without joy. "That's the trap, isn't it?"

steps.why: Naming the hurt and his steady worth helps more than excusing or fixing it.

steps.prompt: Sahil asks: "So how do I stop feeling like a number?"

options.text: "Quit coaching and start fresh somewhere."
options.then: He stares. "Just quit? My parents would collapse."

options.text: "Notice how you treat people. That counts."
options.then: He thinks. "I do stay back to help Jaya with notes."

options.text: "Get a better rank and you'll stop."
options.then: He looks at his shoes. "That's what I was afraid you'd say."

options.text: "Just don't think about it at all."
options.then: He shrugs. "I'll try." He can't stop thinking of it the next hour.

steps.why: Who he is shows in how he treats people, and that holds steady whatever the rank.

scenarios.relearn: A higher rank doesn't make someone a better person.

scenarios.hook: Match each worth-truth to the fear it answers.

scenarios.hook: You graduate next year with no clear plan, and the worry is loud.

steps.prompt: At dinner, your uncle asks about your plan after graduation. What do you do?

options.text: Name the safest job to end the topic
options.then: The topic ends. You're not sure you meant a word of it.

options.text: Say you're exploring, and name one thing you like
options.then: He nods. "Design? Interesting." The pressure eases a little.

options.text: Invent a detailed plan on the spot
options.then: He seems impressed. You worry about keeping up the story.

options.text: Say you've no idea and go quiet
options.then: The table moves on. You feel small and unheard.

steps.why: Saying you're exploring, and naming one interest, is honest and keeps you steady.

steps.prompt: That weekend, you sit with a blank page. What do you do?

options.text: List three things you enjoy and try one
options.then: You pick the easiest. It takes an hour, and the worry has a direction.

options.text: Wait for the perfect career to appear in your head
options.then: You stare at the page. Nothing arrives, and you feel worse.

options.text: List only what pays well
options.then: The list is tidy. It says nothing about what you might enjoy.

options.text: List twenty careers and research them all
options.then: By Sunday night, you've read everything and chosen nothing.

steps.why: Exploring one real interest gives the worry a direction to move in.

steps.prompt: A campus talk is announced on a field you know little about. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it, since you're not sure it's your field
options.then: You skip it. You never learn whether it would have mattered.

options.text: Go and sign up for everything out of panic
options.then: Your name is on six lists. Your week is suddenly full of noise.

options.text: Go only to see what everyone else signs up for
options.then: You copy the crowd. It feels safe, but not yours.

options.text: Go, listen, and note what interests you
options.then: You leave with two questions and a spark of curiosity.

steps.why: Going with curiosity and noting what interests you is how a path shows itself.

scenarios.debrief: You find a path by exploring one real interest at a time, not by thinking harder.
scenarios.relearn: Explore one thing you enjoy this week; a path reveals itself in motion.

myth.why: Skills and interests carry across fields.

scenarios.hook: Your family expects engineering, but you keep getting pulled toward design.

steps.prompt: A free weekend design workshop is announced on campus. What do you do?

options.text: Sign up and treat it as a small test
options.then: You spend Saturday making a poster. It's the best afternoon in weeks.

options.text: Skip it, since engineering is the plan
options.then: The weekend goes by. The pull stays, unanswered.

options.text: Sign up and announce you're switching to design
options.then: Your batchmates are stunned. You haven't even started the workshop, and the news is already travelling.

options.text: Watch the recordings later, when there's more time
options.then: The recordings pile up unwatched. The pull stays theoretical.

steps.why: A small real test tells you more than a hunch or a fight does.

steps.prompt: At home the next weekend, your father asks how college is really going. What do you do?

options.text: Mention design, but call it a passing phase
options.then: He relaxes and laughs. You hear yourself say it, and the pull feels smaller.

options.text: Tell him design is your future now
options.then: He goes silent. "We need to talk about this properly."

options.text: Talk only about engineering, to keep him calm
options.then: He's pleased. You feel like you're playing a part.

options.text: Tell him you want to test design, and why
options.then: He raises an eyebrow, then nods slowly. "Test it how? Show me sometime."

steps.why: Honest, calm sharing, when it feels safe, keeps trust and your options open.

steps.prompt: A friend offers you a small design task for her club. What do you do?

options.text: Take it and plan to drop engineering
options.then: The plan ignores everything else. Your family hears, and panics.

options.text: Take it but call it a hobby that doesn't count
options.then: You finish it fast. The work is good, and you file it away as nothing.

options.text: Take it as a real project to test the pull
options.then: You finish it in a week. You learn what you like and what you don't.

options.text: Decline, in case it distracts from engineering
options.then: She finds someone else. You wonder what you might have learned.

steps.why: A real project gives you evidence about the pull, without staking everything.

scenarios.debrief: You can test a real interest in small steps before you choose, and share it with family when you're ready.
scenarios.relearn: Test a pulling interest with a small real project before you write it off.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the path that fits you can look nothing like the one you pictured at sixteen. That's allowed?
scenarios.affirm: Your sixteen-year-old plan was a guess with less information; updating it is growth, not failure.
scenarios.relearn: The path that fits you can differ from the one you once pictured.

scenarios.hook: Match each small next step to the door it can open.

pairs.left: Emailing one alum to ask about their work
pairs.right: A first honest look inside a field
A skill you can point to
A name and a next conversation

pairs.left: Writing a one-page plan for the month

scenarios.relearn: Each small, concrete step opens a real door; you don't need the whole map to take one.

scenarios.hook: A relative says your only real option is a government job.

steps.prompt: He says it over tea, with everyone listening. What do you do?

options.text: Smile, say nothing, and decide alone later
options.then: He takes your silence as a yes. The matter isn't over.

options.text: Thank him and say you're looking at a few options
options.then: He nods, a little surprised. "At least think about this one."

options.text: Agree that it's the only real option
options.then: Everyone nods. You feel the map shrinking in your chest.

options.text: Tell him he's out of touch
options.then: The room goes silent. Your mother shoots you a look.

steps.why: You can honour the care and still keep your options open.

steps.prompt: Your mother says he means well and asks you to at least apply. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll look into it as one option of several
options.then: She relaxes. "That's all I'm asking." You still have room to explore.

options.text: Promise to apply and quietly drop the rest
options.then: She's delighted. Your other plans shrink without anyone noticing.

options.text: Say you will never apply for one, ever
options.then: She looks hurt. The talk ends coldly.

options.text: Say you'll think about it and change the subject
options.then: She lets it go. The question will return at the next gathering.

steps.why: Treating it as one option among several honours her worry without shrinking your map.

steps.prompt: A friend in a different kind of work offers to show you her day. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it, since you can't afford to explore now
options.then: You stay in. The exploring waits, along with the worry.

options.text: Go and decide on the spot to copy her path
options.then: You're dazzled. By Monday, you see it was built for her.

options.text: Go but ask only about salary
options.then: She answers, a bit puzzled. You learn a number and nothing about the work.

options.text: Go and ask what her work is really like
options.then: She shows you her routine and the boring parts too. It feels real.

steps.why: Seeing real work up close is how you learn what fits you.

scenarios.debrief: Family advice often comes from care and a narrow map; honour the care, widen the map.
scenarios.relearn: You can respect family's worry without accepting their single 'only' path.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a sign a path fits you, or a sign it's a misfit?

items.text: You lose track of time doing it
You dread it every single morning
You only stay for others' approval
It lines up with what you value
It clashes with how you want to live

scenarios.relearn: Losing track of time, curiosity and value-alignment signal fit; daily dread and approval-only signal misfit.

scenarios.hook: Everyone's racing to campus placements, but you want to try a startup.

steps.prompt: The placement list goes up, and your friends are signing up. What do you do?

options.text: Skip placements and call them pointless
options.then: Friends stop inviting you to prep sessions. You feel a bit alone.

options.text: Ask friends what success means and use theirs
options.then: Their answers vary. You realise none of them is yours.

options.text: Write down what success means to you first
options.then: You fill half a page. It's clearer than you expected.

options.text: Sign up for everything so you don't stand out
options.then: Your name is everywhere. Your week fills with things you don't want.

steps.why: Choosing by your own idea of success beats choosing by the crowd.

steps.prompt: A friend says: "Startups are risky. Placements are safe." What do you do?

options.text: Agree and keep the idea as a someday dream
options.then: It stays a "someday" that never gets a date.

options.text: Weigh that and test the startup path on the side
options.then: You try a small project on weekends. It gives you real data.

options.text: Drop the startup idea to avoid the risk
options.then: The idea goes quiet. Some part of you keeps asking about it.

options.text: Call placements a sell-out path
options.then: Your friend bristles. "Some people like stable work, you know."

steps.why: Weighing both, and testing on the side, lets you choose from evidence.

steps.prompt: Placement day arrives and everyone is dressed to impress. What do you do?

options.text: Attend the ones that fit your plan, skip the rest
options.then: You sit for two interviews. You leave feeling clear.

options.text: Follow the crowd into every hall
options.then: You sit through six sessions. You leave tired, and unsure.

options.text: Stay away to prove a point
options.then: You spend the day in the library. The point is lost on everyone.

options.text: Go only to see what everyone else signs up for
options.then: You come home with a list of their choices, not yours.

steps.why: Going only where it fits your plan keeps the choice yours.

scenarios.debrief: The crowd's path fits many and not all; fit, not popularity, is the test.
scenarios.relearn: Choose by your own definition of success, not what the crowd is racing toward.

scenarios.hook: "If I don't choose right now, every door will close."

myth.un: If I don't choose right now, every door closes.
myth.re: Most paths have on-ramps at many ages; pivots and second starts are normal, not closed doors.
myth.why: People change fields throughout working life.

scenarios.relearn: Doors don't all close at once; pivots and later starts are normal routes.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: one small step you take this week counts more than a perfect plan you never start. Pick the step?
scenarios.affirm: A single real step moves you; a perfect unstarted plan moves nothing. Small and started wins.
scenarios.relearn: One small step you actually take beats a perfect plan you never start.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a step that builds your path, or one that just performs for others?

items.text: Learning a skill you'll actually use
Padding your CV with empty titles
Talking to people doing the work
Posting wins you didn't really earn

scenarios.relearn: Real skills, real conversations and small projects build a path; padding and performing for likes don't.

scenarios.hook: A friend's plan looks so sorted that you're tempted to copy it.

steps.prompt: Your friend shares her step-by-step plan for next year. What do you do?

options.text: Ask her to make the same plan for you
options.then: She sighs, but tries. The plan reflects her life, not yours.

options.text: Ask how she built it and what it aims at
options.then: She explains. You see her method and her goals are separate things.

options.text: Copy it exactly and hope it fits
options.then: You copy it neatly. It looks good on paper and feels borrowed.

options.text: Feel behind and say nothing
options.then: You smile and nod. The feeling of being behind sits with you all evening.

steps.why: Learning how she built it lets you borrow her method, not her destination.

steps.prompt: Later you notice her plan has no space for things you enjoy. What do you do?

options.text: Keep her method and add your own interests
options.then: You add a sketching block. The plan feels like yours.

options.text: Drop the plan and feel foolish for looking
options.then: You put the plan away. You feel less sure than before.

options.text: Follow it as is and cut your interests
options.then: The plan runs smoothly. Your week feels grey.

options.text: Ask her to add your interests to her plan
options.then: She tries, politely. The plan grows longer, and further from you.

steps.why: Keeping her method and swapping in your interests makes the plan yours.

steps.prompt: Your parents praise her plan and ask what yours will look like. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll just use hers to end the comparison
options.then: They nod happily. You feel yourself shrinking to fit.

options.text: Say hers is boring and yours will be better
options.then: They frown. "Why the attitude?" The talk turns sour.

options.text: Say nothing and let them assume
options.then: They assume you're copying her. You leave unheard.

options.text: Explain you'll use her method for your interests
options.then: They listen. "That's actually sensible," your mother says.

steps.why: Explaining your reasons calmly shows them a plan that fits you.

scenarios.debrief: A friend's plan fits their values, not yours; take the method, keep your direction.
scenarios.relearn: Borrow a friend's method, not their destination; aim it at your interests.

scenarios.hook: "A values-based path means doing whatever feels good in the moment."

myth.un: A values-based path means chasing whatever feels good right now.
myth.re: It means choosing by what you care about over time, which often asks for steady effort, not just comfort.
myth.why: Values are about direction, not momentary ease.

scenarios.relearn: A values-based path follows what you care about over time, not just momentary comfort.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: you don't owe anyone a five-year plan to be allowed to start. Begin where you are?
scenarios.affirm: You can start with one interest and one step; the five-year plan is optional, not a permission slip.
scenarios.relearn: You can begin where you are; you don't owe anyone a five-year plan first.

scenarios.hook: You're choosing a stream, paralysed by "what if it's wrong".

steps.prompt: Admissions close on Friday and you still can't decide. What do you do?

options.text: Pick the best current fit and plan a review
options.then: You submit it. The knot loosens, and the review date is on your calendar.

options.text: Wait for a sign that it's the right one
options.then: Friday comes with no sign. You pick in a hurry, in a panic.

options.text: Ask ten people and pick the common answer
options.then: Their answers clash. You pick the majority, and feel nothing about it.

options.text: Choose the stream your best friend chose
options.then: You follow her. It feels safe, and not quite yours.

steps.why: A choice you can revise beats waiting for certainty nobody gets.

steps.prompt: Two weeks in, a class is hard and the doubt returns. What do you do?

options.text: Take it as proof you chose wrong
options.then: You tell friends you picked wrong. Your stomach sinks each time you say it.

options.text: Look into switching streams right away
options.then: You spend the week on switching rules. The hard class keeps piling up.

options.text: Hide the struggle and push on alone
options.then: You push through for a month. Falling behind builds quietly.

options.text: Give it a fair few weeks and ask a teacher
options.then: She explains the tough part. It's hard, but doable.

steps.why: Hard weeks are normal. A fair trial and a teacher's help tell you what's real.

steps.prompt: A senior says your direction can shift as you learn, whatever the stream. What do you do?

options.text: Start planning a switch, just in case
options.then: You spend evenings on a plan B. The same doubts come along.

options.text: Doubt the senior and keep worrying
options.then: You shrug off the advice. The worry stays.

options.text: Note your direction can adjust, and keep learning
options.then: The pressure drops. You start noticing what you like.

options.text: Decide you can coast, since it can all change
options.then: You relax too far. Your effort slips, and so does your learning.

steps.why: Knowing your direction can adjust as you learn lets you keep going without panic.

scenarios.debrief: There's rarely one right answer; a good-enough choice you refine beats endless 'what if'.
scenarios.relearn: Pick the best current fit and adjust; you don't need certainty to choose.

scenarios.hook: Match each value to a next step that honours it.

pairs.right: Shadow someone in care or teaching work
Make one small project end to end
Take on one paid freelance task
Join a club or group in that field
Talk to someone solving a problem near home

scenarios.relearn: A values-based step starts from what you care about and turns it into one concrete action.

scenarios.hook: You have no contacts in your field, unlike your richer classmates.

steps.prompt: At lunch, classmates talk about their family contacts. What do you do?

options.text: Decide it's hopeless without connections
options.then: You go quiet at lunch. The day feels heavier than it needs to.

options.text: Wait until someone offers you a chance
options.then: Weeks pass. Nobody knows enough about you to offer anything.

options.text: Scroll their profiles and compare yourself
options.then: An hour later you feel further behind and no closer to a start.

options.text: Pick one skill and share your work publicly
options.then: Your first post gets two likes and a kind comment.

steps.why: You can build a network by making your skills visible.

steps.prompt: You find a person whose work you admire in the field. What do you do?

options.text: Send your CV and ask for a job
options.then: No reply. It's a big ask from a stranger.

options.text: Follow them and like posts, hoping they notice
options.then: They follow you back. The bond goes no further.

options.text: Message them about their work, with one question
options.then: They reply in two days. "Good question. Here's how I'd think about it."

options.text: Wait until you're good enough to be noticed
options.then: The months pass. They never hear of you.

steps.why: A short, specific message is easy to answer and opens a door.

steps.prompt: A stranger at a meetup asks what you're working on. What do you do?

options.text: Ask about her connections first
options.then: She answers briefly. The talk feels like a transaction.

options.text: Say what you're learning and ask a question
options.then: She nods, interested. "Send me what you make. I'll have a look."

options.text: Say it's nothing much yet
options.then: She smiles politely and turns to someone else.

options.text: Exaggerate to sound well connected
options.then: She asks a follow-up. You fumble, and feel exposed.

steps.why: Sharing what you're learning, and asking back, is how networks begin.

scenarios.debrief: No network is a disadvantage, not a verdict; open skills and outreach still open doors.
scenarios.relearn: Without contacts, build skills openly and reach out; you can create a network.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy way to choose a direction, or an anxious one?

items.text: Freezing and letting it decide itself

scenarios.relearn: Steadying first, weighing fit and trying things are healthy; panic-picking, appeasing and freezing are anxious.

scenarios.hook: You want to switch from the "safe" degree your parents chose.

steps.prompt: A class goes badly, and you want to announce the switch tonight. What do you do?

options.text: Quietly stop attending without telling them
options.then: Days pass. The secret makes every meal with them tense.

options.text: Send your mother a long angry text
options.then: She reads it twice. She calls in tears, and the talk goes badly.

options.text: Wait until you're calm, then plan the talk
options.then: You sleep on it. The urge softens, and the wish stays.

options.text: Announce it at dinner while you're upset
options.then: Voices rise. Your father ends it: "We'll talk when you're sensible."

steps.why: Steady first, then raise it: big changes land better from calm.

steps.prompt: A few days later, you're calmer and want to make your case. What do you do?

options.text: Plan to ask them to decide for you
options.then: You hand over the choice. Their answer will be the safe one.

options.text: Write a small plan: why, first steps, a trial
options.then: The page is half a sheet long. It feels solid in your hands.

options.text: List everything wrong with their choice
options.then: The list is long. It's also a fight waiting to happen.

options.text: Prepare to say you'll switch, with or without them
options.then: The line feels strong. It's built for a standoff, not a talk.

steps.why: A small plan shows them a path, not just a wish.

steps.prompt: When you raise it, your father looks worried about it failing. What do you do?

options.text: Hear his worry and share a fallback
options.then: He listens, then nods slowly. "Tell me more about the fallback."

options.text: Promise it will definitely work
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "No one can promise that."

options.text: Say he doesn't understand your generation
options.then: His face closes. The conversation is over before it began.

options.text: Agree it's too risky and offer to drop it
options.then: He relaxes. You feel the wish go quiet inside you.

steps.why: Hearing his worry and sharing a fallback shows care and readiness.

scenarios.debrief: Big changes land better from a steady place with a small plan, not a clash.
scenarios.relearn: Raise a direction change calmly, with a small plan, once you've steadied.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'fit' is a better compass than 'impressive'. Which would you rather follow?
scenarios.affirm: Whatever you picked, notice this: a path that fits you is one you can sustain long after the applause fades.
scenarios.relearn: Fit is a better long-term compass than impressive.

scenarios.hook: "Taking a non-traditional path means I've thrown my degree away."

myth.un: A non-traditional path means I threw my degree away.
myth.re: Skills, discipline and knowledge from a degree travel with you, whatever direction you take next.
myth.why: What you learned doesn't vanish when you pivot.

scenarios.relearn: A non-traditional path doesn't waste your degree; its skills travel with you.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: there isn't one right life waiting to be guessed; there are many that could fit you. Lighter?
scenarios.affirm: Believing there's one secret 'right life' makes every choice terrifying; many good lives could fit you.
scenarios.relearn: There isn't one secret right life to guess; many lives could genuinely fit you.

scenarios.hook: You've drifted for months, scrolling instead of taking a step.

steps.prompt: It's 11pm and you're scrolling again. What do you do?

options.text: Make a giant list of everything to change
options.then: The list is long. It feels impossible by the time you finish.

options.text: Set one tiny action and tell a friend
options.then: She sends a thumbs up. The action is now real.

options.text: Promise yourself a fresh start next Monday
options.then: Monday comes and goes. The promise joins the old ones.

options.text: Scroll on until the guilt fades
options.then: The guilt fades. So does another hour of the night.

steps.why: One tiny action, told to a friend, adds structure and a witness.

steps.prompt: The next day you don't feel motivated. What do you do?

options.text: Do one tiny action anyway, for five minutes
options.then: It takes six minutes. You feel a little lighter.

options.text: Wait until motivation arrives
options.then: You wait. The afternoon drifts, and the feeling doesn't arrive.

options.text: Skip it and promise to do double tomorrow
options.then: Tomorrow's double feels heavier. You scroll instead.

options.text: Tell a friend you'll start later
options.then: She says okay. Later never gets a time.

steps.why: Motivation follows action, so even five minutes counts.

steps.prompt: A week later, a friend asks how things are going. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's all going perfectly well, really
options.then: She cheers. You feel like a fraud.

options.text: Say you've just been far too busy lately
options.then: She nods. The real picture stays hidden.

options.text: Say you'll update her after a big win
options.then: She waits. The win you're waiting on keeps moving away.

options.text: Tell the truth, missed days included
options.then: She nods. "Two out of seven is a start. Want to try for three?"

steps.why: Being honest, missed days and all, keeps you accountable without shame.

scenarios.debrief: Motivation usually follows action; one tiny committed step breaks the drift.
scenarios.relearn: Set one tiny action and tell someone; motivation follows the step, not the wait.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a question that helps you find your direction, or one that traps you?

items.text: "What small thing could I try next?"
"Why can't I have it all figured out?"
"Whose work do I admire and why?"
"What if every choice is a mistake?"

scenarios.relearn: Curious, forward questions help you find direction; comparison and 'all figured out' questions just trap you.

scenarios.hook: You want to test an interest but fear wasting time if it isn't "the one".

steps.prompt: A weekend coding class is open for sign-up. What do you do?

options.text: Sign up and treat the result as information
options.then: You sign up. Whatever happens, you'll know something new.

options.text: Skip it until you're sure it's your thing
options.then: You wait. Sureness doesn't arrive without trying.

options.text: Sign up only if it leads to a job
options.then: You check the job links first. Curiosity shrinks under the conditions.

options.text: Sign up, but count a dull result as failure
options.then: You go, bracing to fail. Every dull minute feels like a verdict.

steps.why: A trial teaches you something either way, so it is never wasted.

steps.prompt: A friend says trying things you may drop is a waste of time. What do you do?

options.text: Agree and stop trying new things
options.then: You stop. Your world gets smaller, until a month later the itch to try returns.

options.text: Get defensive and cut her off
options.then: She goes quiet. The remark stays in your head for days.

options.text: Say you'll only try things you're certain of
options.then: She nods. You quietly realise that list is very short.

options.text: Explain that a "not for me" is useful too
options.then: She thinks. "Huh. So every trial helps narrow it down."

steps.why: A "not for me" narrows the map, and saying so keeps you trying.

steps.prompt: A free month opens up, with time for one trial. What do you do?

options.text: Try three things at once to be sure
options.then: You sample all three. Your month becomes a blur.

options.text: Pick something close to what you already know
options.then: You stay on familiar ground. You learn very little new.

options.text: Pick something you're curious about
options.then: You choose a small photography project. It feels light and alive.

options.text: Pick the trial that looks best on a CV
options.then: It looks strong on paper. You feel little while doing it.

steps.why: Following real curiosity gives you better data than a safe or flashy pick.

scenarios.debrief: A trial that ends in 'not for me' isn't wasted; it narrows the map.
scenarios.relearn: Trying an interest teaches you either way; a 'no' is useful data, not wasted time.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: agency is taking the future from a thing that happens to you to a thing you nudge. Nudge it?
scenarios.affirm: You can't control the whole future, but each small choice nudges it; that nudge is your agency.
scenarios.relearn: Agency is nudging your future with small choices, not controlling all of it.

scenarios.hook: A viral reel insists you must "find your one true passion" or fail.

steps.prompt: The reel leaves you feeling behind. What do you do?

options.text: Panic that you have no single burning passion
options.then: Your chest tightens. The worry grows bigger through the evening.

options.text: Spend the month hunting for your one passion
options.then: You try everything hurriedly. You feel more lost, not less.

options.text: Take the reel's five-step passion quiz
options.then: The quiz says "entrepreneur". You don't feel any closer to anything.

options.text: Close it and notice what you're curious about
options.then: You put the phone down. A few curiosities come to mind.

steps.why: The one-passion rule is a myth, so stepping away from it frees you.

steps.prompt: A friend says she has no single passion, only interests she's building skills in. What do you do?

options.text: Decide she's settling and you won't
options.then: You keep hunting for a big calling, more alone.

options.text: Agree, but keep hunting for yours in secret
options.then: You nod. Inside, the search for the one thing continues.

options.text: Ask how she picks what to work on
options.then: She grins. "I follow what I'm curious about this month."

options.text: Copy her interests, since they work for her
options.then: You sign up for her class. It's her curiosity, not yours.

steps.why: Interest plus growing skill is the real engine, and her approach shows it.

steps.prompt: You try something new and feel only mild interest. What do you do?

options.text: Stop until you feel a burning pull
options.then: You wait for the pull. It doesn't arrive by itself.

options.text: Keep going a little and build the skill
options.then: A few sessions in, the small wins start making it enjoyable.

options.text: Decide it isn't your passion and quit
options.then: You quit after one session. You'll never know how it could have grown.

options.text: Force yourself to love it
options.then: You grit your teeth. It feels like homework, and you feel guilty.

steps.why: Interest often grows with skill, so give it a little time before judging.

scenarios.debrief: The 'one true passion' idea paralyses; interest plus growing skill is the real engine.
scenarios.relearn: You don't need one true passion; build from interest and growing skill.

scenarios.hook: "Asking what fits me is selfish when my family sacrificed so much."

myth.un: Choosing what fits me is selfish after my family's sacrifice.
myth.re: Honouring their sacrifice and choosing a path you can sustain aren't opposites; a path you'll burn out of helps no one.
myth.why: A sustainable path serves you and them.

scenarios.relearn: Choosing a path that fits you isn't selfish; a sustainable path honours their sacrifice too.

items.text: "I get a say in my life"

scenarios.relearn: 'I can choose', 'mine' and 'I get a say' hold your path; 'must', 'not my place' and 'everyone knows better' surrender it.

scenarios.hook: You want to freelance but feel you need permission first.

steps.prompt: A small business asks whether you can design their menu for a fee. What do you do?

options.text: Ask your family whether you may accept
options.then: They hesitate. The deadline passes while they think.

options.text: Take the task and keep it small and clear
options.then: You agree on a price. The brief is one page long.

options.text: Offer to do it free so nobody can object
options.then: She is delighted. A week later, she expects the next one free too.

options.text: Say you're not ready and suggest someone else
options.then: She thanks you politely. You feel a twinge of missed chance.

steps.why: One small paid task builds proof, and proof speaks louder than permission.

steps.prompt: A month later, a friend's shop asks you for a small paid poster. What do you do?

options.text: Say yes and keep a simple record
options.then: Your record has its first lines. It looks like the start of a portfolio.

options.text: Take it, but hide it from the family
options.then: You finish it in secret. The proof exists, but nobody sees it.

options.text: Say yes, but don't count it as real work
options.then: You do it well, then forget it. The proof of your progress fades.

options.text: Ask the family first, then take it
options.then: They grumble but agree. You start late and rush the work.

steps.why: A simple record turns small tasks into visible proof.

steps.prompt: Someone in the family calls freelance not a real job. What do you do?

options.text: Give up to end the argument there
options.then: The air clears. The work you built goes quiet.

options.text: Argue until they finally agree
options.then: You talk for an hour. Nobody changes, and you're tired.

options.text: Ask them for permission to keep freelancing
options.then: They say "We'll see." You're left waiting again.

options.text: Calmly show what you've done so far
options.then: They look it over quietly. "Hm. People are paying you already?"

steps.why: Showing what you've done works better than an argument or another request.

scenarios.debrief: You rarely need universal approval to start; one finished task speaks louder than a debate.
scenarios.relearn: Start one small task; results make a better case than waiting for permission.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the next step doesn't have to be the right step forever, just the next honest one. Take it?
scenarios.affirm: You don't have to get the whole path right; you just have to take the next honest step and keep adjusting.
scenarios.relearn: The next step only has to be the next honest one, not right forever.

scenarios.hook: You're between a stable job and a riskier path you want.

steps.prompt: A stable offer arrives with a one-week deadline. What do you do?

options.text: Delay until you feel completely sure
options.then: The deadline passes. You take a temp job to cover rent while you decide.

options.text: Accept it and test the wanted path on the side
options.then: You sign. On Sunday, you set aside two hours for the new path.

options.text: Turn it down to chase the riskier path
options.then: You decline. Within a week, money panic has you taking a part-time job.

options.text: Bury the want and focus on the stable job
options.then: You push the want away. It returns at odd hours.

steps.why: Testing the wanted path on the side gives you evidence, with a safety net.

steps.prompt: A friend warns you'll be too tired to work and chase the new path too. What do you do?

options.text: Set a small weekly slot and track how it feels
options.then: Two hours on Saturday. By week three, you know how it feels.

options.text: Decide both are impossible and pick one now
options.then: You pick fast. The other path quietly closes.

options.text: Push through every evening with no rest
options.then: You manage a fortnight. Then you crash.

options.text: Work on it only when you feel inspired
options.then: Inspiration comes rarely. The path moves slowly.

steps.why: A small, steady slot is sustainable, and tracking it tells you the truth.

steps.prompt: After a few months, it's time to review your choice. What do you do?

options.text: Decide by gut and leap
options.then: You leap. The feeling is great until the first month's bills arrive.

options.text: Drop the wanted path without looking closer
options.then: You close the file. The question doesn't close with it.

options.text: Ask relatives to vote on it
options.then: The votes split evenly. You feel no closer to knowing.

options.text: Look at what you enjoyed, earned and learned
options.then: Laid side by side, the patterns are clear. The decision feels less scary.

steps.why: Looking at real evidence beats a gut leap or a family vote.

scenarios.debrief: You needn't choose blindly; testing the riskier path alongside the stable one gives evidence.
scenarios.relearn: Test a wanted path on the side first; gather evidence before you leap.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a real reason a path fits, or just a pressure dressed as a reason?
scenarios.relearn: Genuine pull, learning and life-fit are real reasons; silencing questions, expectation and 'everyone' are pressure.

scenarios.hook: You've found a direction, and now you fear telling your parents.

steps.prompt: You've been rehearsing the talk for days. What do you do?

options.text: Prepare one small proof it can work
options.then: You gather a timeline and two examples. It fits on one page.

options.text: Announce it with no plan and brace
options.then: You blurt it out. The room erupts in questions you can't answer.

options.text: Keep it secret until you've succeeded
options.then: You carry it alone. The secret starts to colour every conversation.

options.text: Tell only your mother and ask her to tell him
options.then: She promises to try. She sounds nervous about it too.

steps.why: A small proof of how you'll make it work meets their worry with a plan.

steps.prompt: Your parents hear about it and worry about money and safety. What do you do?

options.text: Say they don't trust you
options.then: Your mother tears up. "We only want you safe."

options.text: Promise it will all be fine
options.then: They look doubtful. "You can't promise that, beta."

options.text: Offer to drop it if they're that worried
options.then: They relax. You feel your direction slip away.

options.text: Acknowledge the worry and answer with specifics
options.then: Your father listens. "At least you've thought about money."

steps.why: Answering worries with specifics honours their love and shows you've thought it through.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, you still want it, and your father still isn't convinced. What do you do?

options.text: Go ahead and stop mentioning it at home
options.then: You begin quietly. Home feels tense whenever it comes up.

options.text: Ask your uncle to convince him
options.then: Your uncle agrees. Your father feels ganged up on, and digs in.

options.text: Start small and offer him regular updates
options.then: He thinks. "All right. Keep me in the loop."

options.text: Take his doubt as a final no and give up
options.then: You put the plan aside. The feeling of loss stays.

steps.why: Starting small and keeping him updated gives him time to settle, while the choice stays yours.

scenarios.debrief: Parents often fear the unknown; a small plan turns your direction into a path they can see.
scenarios.relearn: Share a new direction with one small proof of how you'll make it work.

scenarios.hook: You fear that choosing your own path means losing your family's love.
